**Bulgaria**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-11) officially the **Republic of Bulgaria**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-12) is a country in [Southeastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeastern_Europe "Southeastern Europe"). It is situated on the eastern portion of the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans") directly south of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube") river and west of the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea"). Bulgaria is bordered by [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece") and [Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") to the south, [Serbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serbia "Serbia") and [North Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Macedonia "North Macedonia") to the west, and [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania") across the Danube river to the north. It covers a territory of 110,994 square kilometres (42,855 sq mi), making it the tenth largest within the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") and the [sixteenth-largest country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_European_countries_by_area "List of European countries by area") in Europe by area. [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia") is the nation's capital and [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bulgaria "List of cities and towns in Bulgaria"); other major cities include [Plovdiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv "Plovdiv"), [Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria "Varna, Bulgaria"), and [Burgas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas "Burgas").

One of the earliest societies in the lands of modern-day Bulgaria was the [Karanovo culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karanovo_culture "Karanovo culture") (6,500 BC). In the 6th to 3rd century BC, the region was a battleground for ancient [Thracians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians"), [Persians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persians "Persians"), [Celts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts"), and [Macedonians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Macedonians "Ancient Macedonians"); stability came when the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") conquered the region in AD 45. After the Roman state splintered, tribal invasions in the region resumed. Around the 6th century, these territories were settled by the [early Slavs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Slavs "Early Slavs"). The [Bulgars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars"), led by [Asparuh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asparuh_of_Bulgaria "Asparuh of Bulgaria"), attacked from the lands of [Old Great Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Great_Bulgaria "Old Great Bulgaria") and then permanently invaded the Balkans in the late 7th century. They established the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire"), recognised by treaty in 681 AD by the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"). It dominated most of the Balkans and significantly influenced [Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavs "Slavs") cultures by developing the [Cyrillic script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script "Cyrillic script"). The First Bulgarian Empire lasted until the early 11th century, when Byzantine emperor [Basil II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_II "Basil II") conquered and dismantled it. A [successful Bulgarian revolt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Asen_and_Peter "Uprising of Asen and Peter") in 1185 established a [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire"), which reached its apex under [Ivan Asen II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Asen_II_of_Bulgaria "Ivan Asen II of Bulgaria") (1218–1241). After numerous exhausting wars and feudal strife, the empire disintegrated and in 1396 fell under [Ottoman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") rule for nearly five centuries.

The [Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_of_1877%E2%80%9378 "Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78") resulted in the formation of the third and current Bulgarian state, which declared independence from the Ottoman Empire in 1908. Many ethnic Bulgarians were left outside the new nation's borders, which stoked [irredentist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irredentist "Irredentist") sentiments that led to several conflicts with its neighbours and alliances with [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") in both world wars. In 1946, Bulgaria came under the Soviet-led [Eastern Bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc") and became [a socialist state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Bulgaria "People's Republic of Bulgaria"). The ruling [Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Communist_Party "Bulgarian Communist Party") gave up its monopoly on power after the [revolutions of 1989](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolutions_of_1989 "Revolutions of 1989") and allowed [multiparty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-party_system "Multi-party system") elections. Bulgaria then transitioned into a [democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democracy "Democracy").

Since adopting [a democratic constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_Bulgaria "Constitution of Bulgaria") in 1991, Bulgaria has been a [parliamentary republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_republic "Parliamentary republic") composed of 28 [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Bulgaria "Provinces of Bulgaria"), with a high degree of [political, administrative, and economic centralisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Bulgaria "Government of Bulgaria"). A [developed country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country "Developed country"), its [advanced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_economy "Advanced economy"), [high-income economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/High-income_economy "High-income economy") is part of the [European single market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_single_market "European single market") and is largely based on services, followed by [manufacturing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industry_of_Bulgaria "Industry of Bulgaria"), [mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_in_Bulgaria "Mining in Bulgaria"), and [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_Bulgaria "Agriculture in Bulgaria"). Bulgaria has been influenced by its role as a transit country for [natural gas and oil pipelines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_in_Bulgaria "Energy in Bulgaria"), as well as its strategic [location on the Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Black_Sea_Coast "Bulgarian Black Sea Coast"). Bulgaria is a member state of the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_enlargement_of_the_European_Union "2007 enlargement of the European Union"), including the [Schengen Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area "Schengen Area") and the [eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone "Eurozone"), [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enlargement_of_NATO#Vilnius_Group "Enlargement of NATO"), and various regional suborganizations such as the [Bucharest Nine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bucharest_Nine "Bucharest Nine").

## Etymology

The name _Bulgaria_ is derived from the _[Bulgars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars")_, a tribe of [Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkic_peoples "Turkic peoples") origin that founded the First Bulgarian Empire. Their name is not completely understood and is difficult to trace back earlier than the 4th century AD;[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGolden1992103%E2%80%93104-13) however, it is possibly derived from the [Proto-Turkic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Turkic "Proto-Turkic") word _bulģha_ ("to mix", "shake", "stir") and its derivative _bulgak_ ("revolt", "disorder").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-14) The meaning may be further extended to "rebel", "incite" or "produce a state of disorder", and so, in the derivative, the "disturbers".[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChen201297-15)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-16)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGolden1992104-17) Tribal groups in [Inner Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_Asia "Inner Asia") with phonologically close names were frequently described in similar terms, as the [Buluoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jie_people "Jie people"), a component of the "[Five Barbarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Barbarians "Five Barbarians")" groups, which during the 4th century were portrayed as both: a "mixed race" and "troublemakers".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria#cite_note-FOOTNOTEChen201292%E2%80%9395,_97-18)

The **Stolichna Municipality** ([Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_language "Bulgarian language"): Столична община, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Bulgarian "Romanization of Bulgarian"):_Stolichna obshtina (also transcribed as Stolična obština)_, [lit.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literal_translation "Literal translation")'Capital Municipality') is an [obshtina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obshtina "Obshtina") (_[municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipalities\_of\_Bulgaria "Municipalities of Bulgaria")_) in [Sofia City Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_City_Province "Sofia City Province"), Western [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria"). It is named after its administrative centre, the city of [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia"), which is also the capital of [Sofia City Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_City_Province "Sofia City Province") and [Sofia Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Province "Sofia Province") and the capital of Bulgaria as well.

The municipality is located mainly in the [Sofia Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Valley "Sofia Valley"), and also in the feet and lower parts of the mountains of [Stara planina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stara_planina "Stara planina") and [Vitosha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitosha "Vitosha"), [Plana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plana_(mountain) "Plana (mountain)"), [Lozen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lozen_Mountain "Lozen Mountain"), [Rila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rila "Rila"). As of 2025, the [National Statistical Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Statistical_Institute_(Bulgaria) "National Statistical Institute (Bulgaria)") projected that it was home to 1,232,905 inhabitants, of which 1,205,548 live in Sofia.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stolichna_Municipality#cite_note-2)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Historical name of Sofia, the capital of Bulgaria

This article is about the Roman settlement in today's Sofia, Bulgaria. For the village in Slovenia, see [Serdica, Rogašovci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica,_Roga%C5%A1ovci "Serdica, Rogašovci").

**Serdica** or **Sardica** is the historical [Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") city that was located in today's [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia"), the capital of [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria").

The name is found in the Serdica Fortress in the center of the city, and the [administrative subdivision of Serdika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdika "Serdika").

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Serdica&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts") tribe [Serdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdi "Serdi") gave their name to the city.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-1) The earliest mention of the city comes from an [Athenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens") inscription from the 1st century BC, attesting _Astiu ton Serdon_, i.e. city of the [Serdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdi "Serdi").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-2) A local inscription and [Dio Cassius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dio_Cassius "Dio Cassius") recorded that the Roman general [Crassus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crassus "Crassus") subdued the [Serdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdi "Serdi") and beheaded the captives.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-3)

Around 29 BC, Serdica was conquered by the [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-4)

It gradually became the most important Roman city of the region and became a _[municipium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Municipium "Municipium")_, or centre of an administrative region, during the reign of Emperor [Trajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan "Trajan") (98-117) and was renamed _Ulpia Serdica_.

The city was burnt and destroyed in 170 by the [Costoboci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Costoboci "Costoboci"), and the city was rebuilt, this time with its first defensive walls between 176-180 under [Marcus Aurelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius "Marcus Aurelius"), as evidenced by inscriptions above the gates.

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/Festung_Serdica_Sofia_20090405_012.JPG/250px-Festung_Serdica_Sofia_20090405_012.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Festung_Serdica_Sofia_20090405_012.JPG)

Plan of the Serdica fortress and the archaeological sites. (/\/\) at the top marks the East gate. Legend: 1. Round tower 2. City residence 3. Triangular tower 4. [Banya Bashi Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banya_Bashi_Mosque "Banya Bashi Mosque") 5. [Church of St Petka of the Saddlers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_St_Petka_of_the_Saddlers "Church of St Petka of the Saddlers") 6. [Rotunda of St. George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotunda_of_St._George,_Sofia "Rotunda of St. George, Sofia") 7. Ancient public building 8. Antique complex under the [Bulbank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulbank "Bulbank") building 9. West gate

The city expanded again, as public baths, administrative and cult buildings, a civic [basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica "Basilica") and a large [theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre_of_Serdica "Amphitheatre of Serdica"), were built. When Emperor [Diocletian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian "Diocletian") divided the province of [Dacia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacia "Dacia") into [Dacia Ripensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacia_Ripensis "Dacia Ripensis") (on the banks of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube")) and [Dacia Mediterranea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacia_Mediterranea "Dacia Mediterranea"), Serdica became the capital of the latter.

Roman emperors [Aurelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelian "Aurelian") (215–275)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-5) and [Galerius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galerius "Galerius") (260–311)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-6) were born in Serdica.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Aurelian_Antoninianus%2C_Serdica_Mint%2C_274_A.D.jpg/250px-Aurelian_Antoninianus%2C_Serdica_Mint%2C_274_A.D.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Aurelian_Antoninianus,_Serdica_Mint,_274_A.D.jpg)

Antoninianus of Aurelian minted in Serdica in 274 A.D.

In 268 a Gothic raid ravaged and burned parts of the city including the theatre which was abandoned.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-7)

The city continued to expand and became a significant political and economical centre, more so as it became one of the first Roman cities where Christianity was recognised as an [official religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_religion "State religion"). The [Edict of Serdica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Serdica "Edict of Serdica"), an Edict of Toleration, was issued in 311 in Serdica by the Roman emperor [Galerius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galerius "Galerius"), officially ending the [Diocletianic persecution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletianic_persecution "Diocletianic persecution") of [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity"). The Edict implicitly granted Christianity the status of "religio licita", a worship recognized and accepted by the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"). It was the first edict legalising Christianity, preceding the [Edict of Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Milan "Edict of Milan") by two years. Moreover, in the Edict of Milan, only one sentence was dropped: “Ne quid contra disciplinam agent.” So the Edict of Milan preached unconditional religious tolerance where the Edict of Serdica stated a conditional tolerance (meaning of disciplinam here is: unless they, the christians, disturb the good or social order of the State).

Serdica was the capital of the [Diocese of Dacia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Dacia "Diocese of Dacia") (337-602).

The [amphitheatre of Serdica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre_of_Serdica "Amphitheatre of Serdica") was built over the remains of the theatre under [Diocletian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian "Diocletian") (284–305) and later under [Constantine the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_the_Great "Constantine the Great") (306–337).

For Constantine the Great it was 'Sardica mea Roma est' (Serdica is my Rome). He considered making Serdica the capital of the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") instead of Constantinople.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-9)

The [Tetrarchs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrarchs "Tetrarchs")' and Constantine's efforts to secure a large supply network for the Danube army by building a large number of [horrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horrea "Horrea") in the late 3rd and early 4th centuries appears to have included Serdica as a principal gathering base due to the 8 horrea discovered by excavation.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-10)

In 343, the [Council of Sardica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Sardica "Council of Sardica") was held in a church located where the current 6th century [Church of Saint Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia_Church_(Sofia) "Hagia Sophia Church (Sofia)") was later built.

The city was destroyed by the [Huns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns "Huns") in 447. It was rebuilt by [Byzantine Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Emperor "Byzantine Emperor")[Justinian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian "Justinian") in the 6th century and was renamed Triaditsa.

The city's name was later used for the [Diocese of Sardica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Sardica "Diocese of Sardica").

### Archaeology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Serdica&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Archaeology")]

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/33/Roman_bridge_of_Serdica.jpg/250px-Roman_bridge_of_Serdica.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Roman_bridge_of_Serdica.jpg)

Buttress of Roman bridge of Serdica, 4-6th c.

Many remains of the ancient city have been excavated and are on public display today. These include:

*   _Complex Ancient Serdica_
*   eastern gate
*   western gate
*   city walls
*   thermal baths
*   bridge over the river (near the Lion's bridge)
*   4th c. [church of St. George Rotunda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_St._George,_Sofia "Church of St. George, Sofia")
*   [amphitheatre of Serdica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre_of_Serdica "Amphitheatre of Serdica")
*   the tombs and basilicas under the [basilica of St. Sophia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sophia_Church,_Sofia "Saint Sophia Church, Sofia")

Under Constantine the city expanded to the north of the walls (the so-called Northern Appendix) and the Roman bridge over the river became an important part of this area.

A set of no less than 8 [horrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horrea "Horrea") (warehouses) were found inside the southwestern quarter of the walls and dated to the early 4th century indicate that Serdica was probably a supply-centre of regional importance, connected to the Danube by the valley of the river Iskur (Oescus).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica#cite_note-11)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Serdica&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Legacy")]

[Serdica Peak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica_Peak "Serdica Peak") on [Livingston Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livingston_Island "Livingston Island"), in the [South Shetland Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Shetland_Islands "South Shetland Islands"), [Antarctica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctica "Antarctica"), is named after Serdica.

Serdica is a [titular see](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Titular_see "Titular see") of the [Roman Catholic Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church "Roman Catholic Church").

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Entry for Bulgaria in ISO 3166-2

**ISO 3166-2:BG** is the entry for [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria") in [ISO 3166-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-2 "ISO 3166-2"), part of the [ISO 3166](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166 "ISO 3166")[standard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standardization "Standardization") published by the [International Organization for Standardization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Organization_for_Standardization "International Organization for Standardization") (ISO), which defines [codes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code "Code") for the names of the principal [subdivisions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country_subdivision "Country subdivision") (e.g., [provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Province "Province") or [states](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_(administrative_division) "State (administrative division)")) of all [countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Country "Country") coded in [ISO 3166-1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-1 "ISO 3166-1").

Currently for Bulgaria, ISO 3166-2 codes are defined for [28 districts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_Bulgaria "Provinces of Bulgaria").

Each code consists of two parts, separated by a hyphen. The first part is BG, the [ISO 3166-1 alpha-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-1_alpha-2 "ISO 3166-1 alpha-2") code of Bulgaria. The second part is two digits (01–28). The codes are assigned in [Bulgarian alphabetical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_alphabet "Bulgarian alphabet") order.

# Timeline

_This timeline provides an outline of the major events pertaining to The National’s founding, its trials and tribulations, and the many milestones it has crossed. Periodically you’ll find some entries highlighted in red. These indicates when The National opened after a major renovation or reconstruction project._ _You’ll also notice the occasional entry highlighted in blue. These indicate major events in U.S. history that have transpired in The National’s lifetime. As you can see, the world has changed quite a lot!_

* * *

*     
## 1834

A stockholding company is formed and a board is appointed for the establishment of a new playhouse in Washington. 
*     
## 1835

**July**: William Wilson Corcoran (pictured below) buys and then bequeaths the land on which The National Theatre will be built.

**December 7th:** The National opens with a production of Charles Macklin’s _Man of the World_, staged by Philadelphia’s Chestnut Street Theatre company.

![Image 2: A black and white portrait of William Corcoran.](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/corcoran.jpg)

Historic Figures 
*     
## 1838

Thousands of Cherokee are forced on a deadly march from Georgia to present-day Oklahoma to satisfy the terms of the Indian Removal Act; the passage is known today as the Trail of Tears. 
*     
## 1843

The National is closed for repairs; it reopens and then closes again just a few weeks later; it is converted into a circus and sold to new owners the following year. 
*     
## 1845

The theatre falls under new management and resumes its usual performances…unfortunately, it also catches fire and burns down (not for the last time). 
*     
## 1850

The National is rebuilt by new owners, partly to accommodate the visit of legendary Swedish singer Jenny Lind (pictured below), whose sold-out performances help resurrect the institution. You can learn more about Lind’s time at The National [**here**](https://thenationaldcleadingladies.org/jenny-lind/).

![Image 3: A painted portrait of Jenny Lind, seated with hands folded on her lap.](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/jenny-lind-color.jpg) 
*     
## 1851

**January:**The building is sold again and remodeled as a circus for a French equestrian troupe; the arrangement does not last long.

**December:** Under new management, The National reopens as a theatre again with a performance of Sheridan Knowles’s _The Hunchback_. 
*     
## 1857

After a brief life as “Fanny Morant’s National Theatre” – named after it’s then-manager – The National burns down once again. 
*     
## 1861

The first shots of the Civil War are fired at Fort Sumter in South Carolina, initiating the battle between the Union and the Confederacy over the institution of slavery. 
*     
## 1862

“The New National Theatre” – sometimes called “Grover’s National Theatre” after its manager, Leonard Grover – reopens on its original site.

![Image 4: A black and white drawing of Grover's National Theatre.](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/grovers-national.jpg) 
*     
## 1865

The Civil War ends, and just days later, President Abraham Lincoln is assassinated by actor John Wilkes Booth at Ford’s Theatre; Washington theaters briefly close in mourning. Learn more about Lincoln and Booth’s fateful encounter [**here**](https://thenationaldcpolitics.org/the-booths/). 
*     
## 1873

**January:**Once again, the building catches fire, destroying much of its structure and most of the scenery belonging to a visiting opera company…

**December:** But once again, The National is rebuilt, remodeled, and reopened. 
*     
## 1876

Alexander Graham Bell makes the first telephone call to his assistant, Thomas Watson. 
*     
## 1885

**February:**The National burns down one last time for good measure…

**October:**…And reopens in record time. 
*     
## 1920

The Nineteenth Amendment to the Constitution is ratified, granting women the right to vote.

![Image 5: A black and white photograph of several women waving American flags.](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/suffrage.jpg) 
*     
## 1922

After enjoying a relatively stable period, The National reopens again after significant renovations. 
*     
## 1945

World War II comes to an end after the United States drops atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. 
*     
## 1948

The National closes after management refuses to racially integrate its audiences despite pressure from unions and leading artists; it is later converted to a cinema. Learn more about efforts to desegregate Washington theatres [**here**](https://thenationaldcpolitics.org/desegregation/). 
*     
## 1952

Under new management, The National reemerges as an integrated performing arts institution with a production of _Call Me Madam_, starring the legendary Ethel Merman. 
*     
## 1964

The landmark Civil Rights Act is passed and signed into law by President Lyndon B. Johnson. 
*     
## 1969

Neil Armstrong of the United States becomes the first man to walk on the moon.

![Image 6: Neil Armstrong on the moon with the American flag.](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/armstrong.jpg) 
*     
## 1972

The National Theatre comes under the management of the Nederlander Organization for the first time. 
*     
## 1974

Richard M. Nixon becomes the first, and so far only, President to resign following the Watergate scandal that rocked Washington. Politics has been a consistent feature of life at The National; learn more about that [**here**](https://thenationaldcpolitics.org/presidents-onstage-and-off/).

![Image 7: President Nixon gestures as he](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/nixon.jpg) 
*     
## 1974

A non-profit organization called the New National Theatre Corporation is established to oversee the affairs of The National; it later joins forces with the Kennedy Center for booking services. 
*     
## 1979

After years of working with the Kennedy Center, The National declares its independence. 
*     
## 1980

The New National Theatre Corporation hands management over to the Shubert Organization. 
*     
## 1982

The National closes for extensive renovations after narrowly avoiding demolition as part of an extensive campaign to revitalize Pennsylvania Avenue. 
*     
## 1984

The heavily remodeled National Theatre reopens with a production of the hit musical _42nd Street_ and a brand-new backstage building that includes The National Theatre Archives. President Ronald Reagan gives speech following the curtain, which you can listen to here courtesy of The National Archives:

[Audio 1](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/pp2409-1.mp3)![Image 8: The interior of The National Theatre, photographed in 1984.](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/nat-theatre-1984.jpg)

Structural Changes  
*     
## 1990

Computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee invents the World Wide Web. 
*     
## 1991

The building is closed for several months to allow for the asbestos fire protection curtain to be replaced by a new protection drape. 
*     
## 2008

Barack Obama is elected the first Black President of the United States.

![Image 9: President-elect Barack Obama and family wave to a crowd.](https://thenationaldchistory.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/10/obama.jpeg) 
*     
## 2012

JAM Theatricals and Philadelphia’s SMG assume management from the Shubert Organization. 
*     
## 2019

The Nederlander Organization regains management of The National after acquiring JAM Theatricals. 

## Consider This…

Looking at history requires us not only to examine the past but how that past is presented to us. This is where _historiography_ comes in. Historiography refers to the writing of history and the theories that govern historical study and representation. In putting together this timeline, the dramaturg has had to make decisions about what to include, what to exclude, and how to describe some key moments in the history of The National Theatre and the United States. If you look closely, you might notice a few key themes. Give it some thought and then consider the following questions:

1.   What commonalities can you find between some of the events listed here?
2.   If you were to summarize the message of this timeline, what would it be?
3.   Is there anything missing here that you think just has to be included?

Have something to add? Put it in the comment box below.

# The National Theatre Archive (NTA)

Since its opening in 1835, The National Theatre has played an important role in national and regional performing arts history. The National Theatre Archive works to collect, preserve, and provide access to historical materials which document The National Theatre’s history and impact.

## About

The National Theatre Archive (NTA) was established in 1976 to collect, preserve, and provide access to materials which document The National Theatre’s history and impact. The National Theatre Archive’s holdings include documents, photographs, ephemera, audiovisual recordings, and memorabilia. These materials both document the history of The National Theatre and offer a unique perspective of nearly 200 years of American performing arts trends. NTA is operated by The National Theatre Foundation, the 501(c)(3) non-profit that owns, operates, and preserves The National Theatre.

* * *

Visit our **[Collection Information](https://www.nationaltheatre.org/nta-collection-information/)** page to browse collection contents.

Visit our **[Policies](https://www.nationaltheatre.org/nta-access-policies/)**page for information on how to submit a reference or collection research request.

For donation communications or general inquiries, email us at [information@nationaltheatre.org](mailto:information@nationaltheatre.org) or give us a call at 202-783-3370.

* * *

### Learn more about our amazing partners that make our free community and educational programs possible.

## Teens Behind the Scenes

Meet the [TBTS Dramaturgs](https://www.nationaltheatre.org/meet-the-teens-behind-the-scenes-dramaturgs/) who bring their artistry and expertise to hundreds of students each season.

![Image 11](https://www.nationaltheatre.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2026/03/CSC-7-300x225.jpg)

## The National Theatre’s Community Stages

Get to know our [Roster of Artists](https://www.nationaltheatre.org/community-stage-connections/artist-roster/) who share their talents with audiences who otherwise face barriers to accessing the performing arts.

![Image 12: Hot pink graphic thumbnail design for 2025-2026 Saturday Morning Live! season, with stated theme "Let's Go Exploring!"](https://www.nationaltheatre.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/3/2025/12/2025-26-SML-Post-300x300.jpg)

## Saturday Morning Live!

Check out the [artists lighting up our 2025-26 season](https://www.nationaltheatre.org/introducing-the-2025-26-saturday-morning-live-season/) for small children and their families, all united under the theme of Beyond Borders: What Brings Us Together?

* * *

Maria Ferraguto comes to the National Theatre Foundation with a wealth of experience in non-profit administration, public programming, and strategic communications. Her career began serving public audiences at numerous national institutions, such as the Smithsonian American Art Museum and the National Children’s Museum. Maria demonstrated her organizational skills and resourcefulness as an Exhibit Educator at the National Museum of Natural History. There, she was responsible for designing and facilitating DMV outreach programs that were the first of their kind. She is passionate about using artistic platforms to uplift young and diverse voices, having found her own at a local community theater.

Rebecca Durrant comes to the National Theatre Archives as an archivist and librarian. She holds a Master of Library and Information Science with a specialization in Archives Management and Cultural Heritage. She has professional experience in archives, special collections, and libraries, including the National Gallery of Art Archives and Smithsonian Libraries and Archives.

Rebecca has worked extensively with rare and fragile materials, including manuscripts, fragments, books, photographs, and visual collections, and has experience in archival processing, preservation, and research support for exhibitions, publications, and outreach initiatives. She is passionate about preserving cultural heritage materials and ensuring collections remain accessible for current and future generations to learn from and appreciate.

In her free time, she enjoys reading and gardening with her family.

Beryl Jolly serves as CEO of The National Theatre Foundation, ensuring the preservation and vitality of one of the most illustrious and historical theatres in the country. Ms. Jolly was previously a Vice President at The Trustees of Reservations, overseeing cultural properties throughout Massachusetts. She also served as the Executive Director of the Mahaiwe Performing Arts Center in the Berkshires of western Massachusetts, presenting headliner talents of diverse genres to hundreds of thousands of audience members.

Ms. Jolly has worked in management roles in theatres on and off-Broadway, and in fundraising and development at the Brooklyn Academy of Music (BAM). She received a Massachusetts Senate Citation for fifteen years of superior artistic leadership as Executive Director of the Mahaiwe Performing Arts Center and served on the Berkshire Regional Planning Commission’s Economic Development Strategy Committee. She currently serves on the Jewish Federation of the Berkshires Board of Directors.

202.783.3371 (o)

Photo by Christine Lane Photography

As a passionate and dedicated professional in the non-profit world, Kati brings over 12 years of experience in operations, development and event management fields. With a Bachelor of Arts Degree in Interdisciplinary Studies from Arizona State University, she likes to make connections and always tries to find the best path for any project. Spending 12 years on Capitol Hill at the Congressional Award Foundation, Congress’ Award for Young People, she worked tirelessly with young people, mentors, Members of Congress, Board Members and business leaders in recognizing the volunteer work of America’s Youth. After The Congressional Award, she volunteered with Alexandria, Virginia schools in fundraising and events and served as a Parents Association President and School Board Member for two years.

Kati loves to be extra because life is too short to not enjoy it. She loves a good theme party, any excuse for celebration and spending time at home in Alexandria with her three boys and husband.

Damian Sinclair returns to the Washington DC arts community as the Director of Development for the National Theatre Foundation. Previously, he founded the Capital Fringe Festival in the Nation’s capital to create an outlet for artists to experiment. Additionally, he helped open two new performance venues with Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company and Arena Stage. He is the author of The Simple Art of Fundraising, a book designed to give artists the confidence to go out and raise the financial support they need. He has worked with and supported some of the country’s most exciting groups including: Philadelphia’s Pig Iron Theatre Company, New Paradise Laboratories, Headlong Dance Theater; Austin’s Rude Mechs; Humboldt County’s own Dell Arte and numerous other artists and groups.

Carey comes to the National Theatre Foundation bringing experience as an arts administrator, non-profit financial manager, and theatre professional. Her background includes a BFA in Music Theatre from Shenandoah Conservatory and an MS in Arts Administration from Boston University. She began her career as an Equity stage manager, theater rentals coordinator and assistant box office manager. Upon receiving her master’s degree, she served as Manager of Music Department Operations at George Washington University, and Fiscal Operations Manager with the Corcoran School of Arts and Design, and she most recently comes to us from Green Hedges School where she was Director of Finance and Operations.

Jared Strange joined The National Theatre Foundation as the Education and Community Programs Manager in May of 2023, and previously worked as Dramaturg for Teens Behind the Scenes from 2019 to 2022. He holds a PhD in Theatre and Performance Studies from the University of Maryland, where he was a Mary Savage Snouffer fellow, and an MFA in Playwriting from Texas Tech University, where he later served as the Arts Coordinator for the $24.5million East Lubbock Promise Neighborhood Grant. Jared writes locally for _Washington City Paper_ and _DC Theatre Arts_; his articles and reviews can also be found in _American Theatre_ magazine, _3Views on Theater_, _Theatre Research International_, _Journal of Dramatic Theory and Criticism_, _Comparative Drama_, and _Theatre Journal_. As a playwright, dramaturg, and director, Jared specializes in new play development, audience engagement, and educational programming, and has developed projects across the United States and in Europe. His educational career has seen him teach students of all ages, devise and implement a range of arts enrichment programs, and work locally with such organizations as Young Playwrights’ Theater.

Photo by Kevin Allen Photo

Paul Reagan brings a wealth of experience to his role as Director of Operations at the National Theatre Foundation, having assumed the position in December 2023. Before joining our organization, he served as the Operations Director at Arena Stage, where his responsibilities included the oversight of capital projects and daily building operations.

Paul played a pivotal role in the successful reopening of the theater in 2021, demonstrating his adept management skills in ensuring the safety of both patrons and staff. His tenure at Arena Stage was marked by his leadership in executing renovations and capital projects, thereby elevating the overall experience for both patrons and staff members.

With a proven track record of effective operations management and a commitment to enhancing the operational efficiency of cultural institutions, his expertise and dedication contribute significantly to the advancement of our organization’s mission and objectives.

# NTA Access Policies

## Equity Statement

The National Theatre Archive (NTA) makes its resources and services available to the general public. We strive to facilitate equitable and inclusive access to the collection and to accommodate all inquiries to the best of our ability.

## Accessing the Collection

Please submit reference and research inquiries to [information@nationaltheatre.org](mailto:information@nationaltheatre.org).

To browse The National Theatre Archive’s collection, refer to the **Collection Finding Aid** and container lists located within the**[Collection Information](https://www.nationaltheatre.org/nta-collection-information/)**page.

Records in the collection which contain confidential or personally identifiable information are closed for research purposes. Locations of restricted records are noted in both the **Collection Finding Aid** and within the individual container lists.

Currently, The National Theatre Archive does not provide on-site research services. Special requests for in-person access to the collection should be directed to [information@nationaltheatre.org](mailto:information@nationaltheatre.org) and are subject to approval by the Executive Director.

## Requesting Access Copies

A digital access copy is a reproduction of an archival item delivered as a digital file. Researchers may request digital access copies of any non-restricted materials within the collection.

Please submit access copy requests to [information@nationaltheatre.org](mailto:information@nationaltheatre.org).

A service fee may be charged for high-volume copy requests. A representative of The National Theatre Foundation will communicate the estimated time needed to process the request as well as any applicable fees in advance.

## Loan of Materials

Currently, The National Theatre Archive does not loan out collection materials.

In some circumstances, The National Theatre Archive may temporarily loan original archival materials for exhibition. Loan requests are subject to the approval by the Chief Executive Officer.

**Plovdiv** ([Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_language "Bulgarian language"): Пловдив, pronounced[[ˈpɫɔvdif]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Bulgarian "Help:IPA/Bulgarian")) is the [second-largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bulgaria "List of cities and towns in Bulgaria") in [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria") and the most populous city in the [Bulgarian part](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Thrace "Northern Thrace") of the historic region of [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace "Thrace"), located 144 km (93 miles) southeast of the capital [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia"). It is considered the [oldest European continually inhabited city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_oldest_continuously_inhabited_cities#Europe "List of oldest continuously inhabited cities"), having been inhabited since c. 6,000 BCE. It had a population of 329,489 as of 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Plovdiv&action=edit) and 540,000 in its greater metropolitan area. An important economic, transport, cultural, and educational hub of Bulgaria, Plovdiv was the [European Capital of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Capital_of_Culture "European Capital of Culture") in 2019, and joined the UNESCO Global Network of Learning Cities in 2016.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-UNESCO_UIL-GNLC-4)

Plovdiv is in a fertile region of south-central Bulgaria on the two banks of the [Maritsa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritsa_River "Maritsa River"). The city has historically developed on seven [syenite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syenite "Syenite") hills, some of which are 250 metres (820 feet) high. Because of these hills, Plovdiv is often referred to in Bulgaria as "The City of the Seven Hills". There is evidence of habitation in the area dating back to the 6th millennium BC, when the first [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") settlements were established. The city was subsequently a [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians") settlement named Pulpudeva, later being conquered and ruled also by [Persians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire"), [Ancient Macedonians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Macedonians "Ancient Macedonians"), [Celts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_settlement_of_Southeast_Europe "Celtic settlement of Southeast Europe"), [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), [Byzantines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire"), [Goths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goths "Goths"), [Huns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns "Huns"), [Bulgarians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarians "Bulgarians"), [Thraco-Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thraco-Roman "Thraco-Roman"), [Bulgars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars"), [Slavic tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Slavic_tribes "Seven Slavic tribes"), [Crusaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Empire "Latin Empire"), and [Ottoman Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-plovdiv1-5)

Philippopolis ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Φιλιππούπολις) was founded as a _[polis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polis "Polis")_ by the father of [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great"), [Philip the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_the_Great "Philip the Great") (r.359–336 BC), the king of ancient [Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(ancient_kingdom) "Macedonia (ancient kingdom)"), settling there both Thracians and 2,000 [Macedonians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Macedonians "Ancient Macedonians") ([Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greeks "Ancient Greeks")) in 342 BC.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:0-6) Control of the city alternated between the Macedonian kingdom and the Thracian [Odrysian kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysian_kingdom "Odrysian kingdom") during the [Hellenistic period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_period "Hellenistic period"); the Macedonian king [Philip V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Macedon "Philip V of Macedon") (r.221–179 BC) reoccupied the city in 183 BC and his successor [Perseus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perseus_of_Macedon "Perseus of Macedon") (r.179–168 BC) held the city with the Odrysians until the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") conquered the Macedonian kingdom in 168 BC.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:0-6) Philippopolis became the capital of the [Roman province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_province "Roman province") of [Thracia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracia "Thracia").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:0-6) The city was at the centre of the road network of inland Thrace, and the strategic _[Via Militaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via\_Militaris "Via Militaris")_ was crossed by several other roads at the site, leading to the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube"), the [Aegean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_Sea "Aegean Sea"), and the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea"). The [Roman emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_emperor "Roman emperor")[Marcus Aurelius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Aurelius "Marcus Aurelius") (r.161–180 AD) built a new [wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_wall "Defensive wall") around the city.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:0-6)

In [Late Antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Antiquity "Late Antiquity"), Philippopolis was an important stronghold, but was sacked in 250 during the [Crisis of the Third Century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Third_Century "Crisis of the Third Century"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:0-6) after the [Siege of Philippopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Philippopolis_(250) "Siege of Philippopolis (250)") by the [Goths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goths "Goths") led by [Cniva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cniva "Cniva"). After this the settlement contracted, though it remained a major city, with the city walls rebuilt and new Christian [basilicas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilicas "Basilicas") and [Roman baths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_baths "Roman baths") constructed in the 4th century.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:2-8) The city was again sacked by the [Huns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns "Huns") in 441/442, and the walls were again rebuilt.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:2-8) Roman Philippopolis resisted another attack, by the [Avars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Avars "Pannonian Avars") in the 580s, after the walls were renewed yet again by [Justinian the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_the_Great "Justinian the Great") (r.527–565).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:2-8)

In the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), Philippopolis fell to the [Bulgars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars") of the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire") in 863, during the reign of [Boris I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_I "Boris I") (r.852–889), having been briefly abandoned by the Christian inhabitants in 813 during a dispute with the _[khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan\_of\_Bulgaria "Khan of Bulgaria")_[Krum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krum "Krum") (r.c.803–814).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:2-8)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) During the [Byzantine–Bulgarian wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine%E2%80%93Bulgarian_wars "Byzantine–Bulgarian wars"), the emperor [Basil the Bulgar-Slayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_the_Bulgar-Slayer "Basil the Bulgar-Slayer") (r.960–1025) used Philippopolis as a major strategic fortification, governed by the _[protospatharios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protospatharios "Protospatharios")_[Nikephoros Xiphias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikephoros_Xiphias "Nikephoros Xiphias").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) In the middle 11th century, the city was attacked by the [Pechenegs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pechenegs "Pechenegs"), who occupied it briefly around 1090.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) The city continued to prosper, with the walls restored in the 12th century, during which the historian and politician [Niketas Choniates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niketas_Choniates "Niketas Choniates") was its governor and the physician [Michael Italikos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Italikos "Michael Italikos") was its [metropolitan bishop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_bishop "Metropolitan bishop").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7)

According to the Latin historian of the [Fourth Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade "Fourth Crusade"), [Geoffrey of Villehardouin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_of_Villehardouin "Geoffrey of Villehardouin"), Philippopolis was the third largest city in the Byzantine Empire, after [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople") ([Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul")) and [Thessalonica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessalonica "Thessalonica") ([Thessaloniki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessaloniki "Thessaloniki")).[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) It suffered damage from the armies passing through the city during the [Crusades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades "Crusades") as well as from sectarian violence between the [Eastern Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox "Eastern Orthodox") and the [Armenian Orthodox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenian_Orthodox "Armenian Orthodox") and [Paulician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paulician "Paulician") denominations.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) The city was destroyed by [Kaloyan of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaloyan_of_Bulgaria "Kaloyan of Bulgaria") (r.1196–1207) in 1206 and rebuilt thereafter.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) In 1219, the city became the capital of the Crusader [Duchy of Philippopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Philippopolis "Duchy of Philippopolis"), part of the [Latin Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Empire "Latin Empire").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) The [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire") recovered the city in 1263, but lost it to Byzantine control before recapturing it in 1323.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) The [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") conquered Philippopolis ([Turkish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish_language "Turkish language"): _Filibe_) in 1363 or 1364.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-:1-7) During the 500 years of Ottoman rule, Filibe served as one of the important commercial and transportation nodes in the Ottoman Balkans. It also played a role as an administrative centre of various [sanjaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjak "Sanjak") and [eyalets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eyalet "Eyalet").

On 4 January 1878, at the end of the [Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_(1877%E2%80%931878) "Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)"), Plovdiv was taken away from Ottoman rule by the [Russian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russian_Empire "Russian Empire") army. It remained within the borders of Bulgaria until July of the same year, when it became the capital of the autonomous Ottoman region of [Eastern Rumelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Rumelia "Eastern Rumelia"). In 1885, Plovdiv and Eastern Rumelia [joined](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_unification "Bulgarian unification") Bulgaria.

There are many preserved ruins such as the ancient [Plovdiv Roman theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv_Roman_theatre "Plovdiv Roman theatre"), a Roman [odeon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odeon_(building) "Odeon (building)"), a [Roman aqueduct](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_aqueduct "Roman aqueduct"), the [Plovdiv Roman Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv_Roman_Stadium "Plovdiv Roman Stadium"), the archaeological complex Eirene, and others. Plovdiv is host to a huge variety of cultural events such as the [International Fair Plovdiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Fair_Plovdiv "International Fair Plovdiv"), the international theatrical [festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Festival "Festival") "A stage on a crossroad", the TV festival "The golden chest", and many more novel festivals, such as Night/Plovdiv in September, Kapana Fest, and Opera Open. The oldest American educational institution outside the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), the [American College of Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_College_of_Sofia "American College of Sofia"), was founded in Plovdiv in 1860 and later moved to Sofia.

## Etymology

Plovdiv has been given various names throughout its long history. The [Odrysian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysian_kingdom "Odrysian kingdom") capital _Odrysa_ ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Οδρύσα), is suggested to have been modern Plovdiv by numismatic research[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-arc-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-10) or [Odrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edirne "Edirne") (Adrianople).[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-academia-11) The Greek historian [Theopompus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theopompus "Theopompus")[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-theopompi-12) mentioned it in the 4th century BC as a town named _Poneropolis_ ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Πονηρόπολις) "town of villains") in pejorative relation to the conquest by king [Philip II of Macedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Macedon "Philip II of Macedon") who is said to have settled the town with 2,000 men who were false-accusers, sycophants, lawyers, and other possible disreputables.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-13) According to [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch "Plutarch"), the town was named by this king after he had populated it with a crew of rogues and vagabonds,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-14) but this is possibly a folk name that did not actually exist.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-academia-11) The names _Dulon polis_ ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Δουλωνπολις "slaves' town") and possibly _Moichopolis_ ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Μοιχοπολις "adulterer's town") likely have similar origins.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The city has been called _Philippopolis_ (Φιλιππόπολις) pronounced[[pʰilipopolis]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Greek "Help:IPA/Greek"); Modern [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Φιλιππούπολη, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Greek "Romanization of Greek"):_Philippoupoli_ pronounced[[filipupoli]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Greek "Help:IPA/Greek")) or "the city of Philip", from [Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Φίλιππος, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Ancient_Greek "Romanization of Ancient Greek"):_Philippos_ "horse-lover", most likely in honor of [Philip II of Macedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Macedon "Philip II of Macedon")[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-col-15) after his death or in honor of [Philip V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Macedon "Philip V of Macedon"),[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-arc-9)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-pld-16) as this name was first mentioned in the 2nd century BC by [Polybius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polybius "Polybius") in connection with the campaign of Philip V.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-arc-9)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-pld-16)_Philippopolis_ was identified later by [Plutarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plutarch "Plutarch") and [Pliny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder "Pliny the Elder") as the former _Poneropolis_. [Strabo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strabo "Strabo") identified Philip II's settlement of most "evil, wicked" (Modern [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): πονηροτάτους, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Greek "Romanization of Greek"):_ponerotatous_ ) as Cabyle ([Kabyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabyle_(ancient_city) "Kabyle (ancient city)")),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-17) whereas [Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy") considered the location of Poneropolis different from the rest.

_Kendrisia_ ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Κενδρεισεία) was an old name of the city.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-plovdiv1-5) Its earliest recorded use is on an artifact mentioning that king [Beithys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beithys "Beithys"), priest of the Syrian goddess, brought gifts to Kendriso [Apollo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apollo "Apollo");[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-18) the deity is recorded to be named multiple times after different cities. Later Roman coins mentioned the name which is possibly derived from Thracian god Kendriso who is equated with Apollo,[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-19) the [cedar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cedrus "Cedrus") forests, or from the Thracian tribe artifacts known as the kendrisi.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-plovdiv1-5)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-pld-16) Another assumed name is the 1st century AD _Tiberias_ in honor of the Roman emperor [Tiberius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tiberius "Tiberius"), under whom the [Odrysian Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysian_Kingdom "Odrysian Kingdom") was a [client](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Client_state "Client state") of Rome.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-academia-11) After the Romans had taken control of the area, the city was named in [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _Trimontium_, meaning "The Three Hills", and mentioned in the 1st century by [Pliny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder "Pliny the Elder"). At times the name was _[Ulpia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulpia\_gens "Ulpia gens")_, _[Flavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flavia\_gens "Flavia gens")_, _[Julia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julia\_gens "Julia gens")_ after the Roman families.

[Ammianus Marcellinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammianus_Marcellinus "Ammianus Marcellinus") wrote in the 4th century AD that the then city had been the old _Eumolpias_/_Eumolpiada,_,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-20) the oldest name chronologically.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-academia-11) It was named after the mythical Thracian king [Eumolpos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eumolpos "Eumolpos"), son of [Poseidon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poseidon "Poseidon")[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-21) or [Jupiter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jupiter_(mythology) "Jupiter (mythology)"),[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-22) who may have founded the city around 1200 BC [[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-23) or 1350 BC.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-24) It is also possible that it was named after the [Vestal Virgins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestal_Virgins "Vestal Virgins") in the temples – evmolpeya.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-plovdiv1-5)

In the 6th century AD, [Jordanes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jordanes "Jordanes") wrote that the former name of the city was _Pulpudeva_ and that [Philip the Arab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_the_Arab "Philip the Arab") named the city after himself. This name is most likely a [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracian_language "Thracian language") oral translation[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-plovdiv1-5) of the other as it kept all consonants of the name Philip + [deva (city)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dava_(Dacian) "Dava (Dacian)"). Although the two names sound similar, they may not share the same origin as [Adrianople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrianople "Adrianople") does, and _Pulpudeva_ may have predated the other names[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-uk-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-26) meaning "lake city" in [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracian_language "Thracian language").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-pld-16) Since the 9th century AD the Slavic name began to appear as _Papaldiv/n, Plo(v)div, Pladiv, Pladin, Plapdiv, Plovdin,_ which originate from _Pulpudeva_.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-27) As a result, the name has lost any meaning. In British English the Bulgarian variant Пловдив _Plòvdiv_ has become prevalent after [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The [Crusaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusaders "Crusaders") mentioned the city as _Prineople_, _Sinople_ and _Phinepople_.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-pld-16) The Ottomans called the city _Filibe_, a corruption of "Philip", in a document from 1448.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-28)

The history of the region spans more than eight millennia. Numerous nations have left their traces on the twelve-metre-thick (39-[foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foot_(unit) "Foot (unit)")) cultural layers of the city. The earliest signs of habitation in the territory of Plovdiv date as far back as the 6th millennium BC.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-filipopol-29)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-plovdiv1-5) Plovdiv has settlement traces including necropolises dating from the Neolithic era (roughly 6000–5000 BC) like the mounds Yasa Tepe 1 in the Philipovo district and Yasa Tepe 2 in Lauta park.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-%D1%80%D0%B0%D0%B9%D1%87%D0%B5%D0%B2%D1%81%D0%BA%D0%B8-30)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-%D0%BA%D0%B5%D1%81%D1%8F%D0%BA%D0%BE%D0%B2%D0%B0-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-32)

Archaeologists have discovered fine pottery[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] and objects of everyday life on [Nebet Tepe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nebet_Tepe "Nebet Tepe") from as early as the [Chalcolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalcolithic "Chalcolithic") era, showing that at the end of the 4th millennium BC, there was already an established settlement there which was [continuously inhabited](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_oldest_continuously_inhabited_cities "List of oldest continuously inhabited cities") since then.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-35) Thracian necropolises dating back to the 2nd–3rd millennium BC have been discovered, while the Thracian town was established between the 2nd and the 1st millennium BC.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The town was a fort of the independent local [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians") tribe [Bessi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessi "Bessi").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-36) In 516 BC during the rule of [Darius the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darius_the_Great "Darius the Great"), Thrace was included in the [Persian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-37) In 492 BC, the Persian general [Mardonius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mardonius_(general) "Mardonius (general)") subjugated Thrace again, and it nominally became a vassal of Persia until 479 BC and the early rule of [Xerxes I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerxes_I "Xerxes I").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-38) The town became part of the [Odrysian kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysian_kingdom "Odrysian kingdom") (460 BC – 46 AD), a [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians") tribal union. The town was conquered by [Philip II of Macedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Macedon "Philip II of Macedon"),[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-39) and the Odrysian king was deposed in 342 BC. Ten years after the Macedonian invasion, the Thracian kings started to exercise power again after the Odrysian [Seuthes III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seuthes_III "Seuthes III") had re-established their kingdom under Macedonian suzerainty as a result of a successful revolt against [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great")'s rule resulting in a stalemate.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-40) The Odrysian kingdom gradually overcame the Macedonian suzerainty, while the city was destroyed by the [Celts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts") as part of the [Celtic settlement of Eastern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_settlement_of_Eastern_Europe "Celtic settlement of Eastern Europe"), most likely in the 270s BC.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-41) In 183 BC, [Philip V of Macedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_V_of_Macedon "Philip V of Macedon") conquered the city, but shortly after, the Thracians re-conquered it.

In 72 BC, the city was seized by the Roman general [Marcus Lucullus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcus_Terentius_Varro_Lucullus "Marcus Terentius Varro Lucullus") but was soon restored to Thracian control. In 46 AD, the city was finally incorporated into the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") by emperor [Claudius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudius "Claudius");[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-42) it served as the capital of the province of [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace "Thrace"). Although it was not the capital of the province of Thrace, the city was the largest and most important centre in the province.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-43) As such, the city was the seat of the Union of Thracians.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-44) In those times, the [Via Militaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Militaris "Via Militaris") (or Via Diagonalis), the most important military road in the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"), passed through the city.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-46) The Roman times were a period of growth and cultural excellence.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-47) The ancient ruins tell a story of a vibrant, growing city with numerous public buildings, shrines, baths, theatres, a stadium, and the only developed ancient water supply system in Bulgaria. The city had an advanced water system and [sewerage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanitary_sewer "Sanitary sewer").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] In 179 a second wall was built to encompass Trimontium which had already extended out of the Three hills into the valley. Many of those are still preserved and can be seen by tourists. Today only a small part of the ancient city has been excavated.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-pldiv-48)

In 250 the city was captured and looted after the [Battle of Philippopolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Philippopolis_(250) "Battle of Philippopolis (250)") by the [Goths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goths "Goths"), led by their ruler [Cniva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cniva "Cniva"). Many of its citizens, 100,000 according to [Ammianus Marcellinus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ammianus_Marcellinus "Ammianus Marcellinus"), died or were taken captive.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-49) It took a century and hard work to recover the city. However, it was destroyed again by [Attila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attila "Attila")'s [Huns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hun "Hun") in 441–442 and by the [Goths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goths "Goths") of [Theodoric Strabo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodoric_Strabo "Theodoric Strabo") in 471.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-50)

An ancient Roman inscription written in Ancient Greek dated to 253 – 255 AD were discovered in the [Great Basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Basilica,_Plovdiv "Great Basilica, Plovdiv"). The inscription refers to the [Dionysian Mysteries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionysian_Mysteries "Dionysian Mysteries") and also mentions Roman Emperors [Valerian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valerian_(emperor) "Valerian (emperor)") and [Gallienus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallienus "Gallienus"). It has been found on a large stele which was used as construction material during the building of the Great Basilica.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-51)

In August 2024, archaeologists from the Regional Archaeological Museum announced the discovery of a well-preserved Thracian temple dated to the third century BC. The 10-metre-long temple is made of dry joints and clay-sand mortar and has two rooms.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv#cite_note-53)

**Varna** ([Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_language "Bulgarian language"): Варна, pronounced[[ˈvarnɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Bulgarian "Help:IPA/Bulgarian")) is the [third-largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bulgaria "List of cities and towns in Bulgaria") in [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria") and the largest city and [seaside resort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaside_resort "Seaside resort") on the [Bulgarian Black Sea Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Black_Sea_Coast "Bulgarian Black Sea Coast") and in the [Northern Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Bulgaria "Northern Bulgaria") region. Situated strategically in the [Gulf of Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Varna "Gulf of Varna"), the city has been a major economic, social, and cultural centre for almost three millennia. Historically known as _Odessos_ ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ὀδησσός), Varna developed from a [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians") seaside settlement into a major [seaport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seaport "Seaport") on the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea").

Varna is a significant hub for business, transportation, education, tourism, entertainment, and healthcare. The city is referred to as the maritime capital of Bulgaria and is home to the headquarters of the [Bulgarian Navy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Navy "Bulgarian Navy") and merchant marine. In 2008, Varna was designated as the seat of the [Black Sea Euroregion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea_Euroregion "Black Sea Euroregion") by the [Council of Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Europe "Council of Europe").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-2) In 2014, Varna was awarded the title of [European Youth Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Youth_Capital "European Youth Capital") 2017.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-3)

The oldest gold treasure in the world, belonging to the [Varna culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_culture "Varna culture"), was discovered in the [Varna Necropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_Necropolis "Varna Necropolis") and dated to 4600–4200 BC.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-4) Since the discovery of the Varna Necropolis in 1974, 294 burial sites have been excavated, with over 3000 golden items inside.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-5)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]
