[Theophanes the Confessor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theophanes_the_Confessor "Theophanes the Confessor") first mentions the name _Varna_, as the city came to be known, within the context of the [Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavs "Slavs") conquest of the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans") in the 6th to 7th centuries. The name could be of [Varangian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varangian "Varangian") origin, as Varangians had been crossing the Black Sea for many years, reaching [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople") in the early Middle Ages. In [Swedish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_language "Swedish language"), _värn_ means 'shield, defense'– hence Varna could mean 'defended, fortified place'. Vikings invaded the settlement during the Middle Ages.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-6) The name may be older than that; perhaps it derives from the [Proto-Indo-European root](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Indo-European_root "Proto-Indo-European root")_*u̯er-_ 'to flow, wet, water, river'[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-8) (cf. [Varuna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varuna "Varuna")), or from the [Proto-Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-Slavic "Proto-Slavic") root _varn_ 'black', or from [Iranian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iranian_languages "Iranian languages")_bar_ or _var_ 'camp, fortress' (see also [Etymological list of provinces of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etymological_list_of_provinces_of_Bulgaria "Etymological list of provinces of Bulgaria")).

According to Theophanes, in 680, [Asparukh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asparuh_of_Bulgaria "Asparuh of Bulgaria"), the founder of the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire"), routed an army of [Constantine IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_IV "Constantine IV") near the Danube River delta. Pursuing those forces, he reached "the so-called Varna near Odyssos [_[sic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sic "Sic")_] and the midlands thereof" (τὴν λεγομένην Βάρναν, πλησίον Ὀδυσσοῦ). Perhaps the new name applied initially to an adjacent river or lake, a Roman military camp, or an inland area, and only later to the city itself.

By the late 10th century, the name _Varna_ was established so firmly that when Byzantines wrested back control of the area from the Bulgarians around 975, they kept it rather than restoring the ancient name _Odessos_.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

See also: [Timeline of Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Varna "Timeline of Varna")

### Prehistory

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Prehistory")]

See also: [Varna Necropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_Necropolis "Varna Necropolis")

Prehistoric settlements are best known for the [Chalcolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalcolithic "Chalcolithic")[necropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_Necropolis "Varna Necropolis") (mid-5th millennium BC radiocarbon dating), a key archaeological site in world prehistory, the eponymous [Varna culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_culture "Varna culture"), and internationally regarded as the world's oldest large find of gold artifacts, which existed within modern city limits. In the wider region of the Varna lakes (before the 1900s, freshwater) and the adjacent [karst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karst "Karst") springs and caves, over 30 prehistoric settlements have been unearthed, with the earliest artefacts dating back to the [Middle Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Paleolithic "Middle Paleolithic") or 100,000 years ago.

### Thracians

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Thracians")]

Since the late [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") (13th–12th c. BC), the area around Odessos had been populated with [Thracians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians"). During the 8th–9th c. BC local [Thracians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians") had active commercial and cultural contacts with people from [Anatolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatolia "Anatolia"), [Thessaly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessaly "Thessaly"), the [Caucasus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caucasus "Caucasus"), and the [Mediterranean Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mediterranean_Sea "Mediterranean Sea"). These links were reflected in some local productions, for example, forms of bronze [fibula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fibula_(brooch) "Fibula (brooch)") of the age, either imported or locally made. There is no doubt that interactions occurred mostly by sea, and the bay of Odessos is one of the places where the exchanges took place. Some scholars consider that during the 1st millennium BC, the region was also settled by the half-mythical [Cimmerians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cimmerians "Cimmerians"). An example of their, probably accidental, presence is the [tumulus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus "Tumulus") dated 8th–7th c. BC found near [Belogradets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belogradets "Belogradets"), Varna Province.

The region around Odessos was densely populated with Thracians long before the coming of the Greeks to the western seashore of the Black Sea. [Pseudo-Scymnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Scymnus "Pseudo-Scymnus") writes: "...Around the city [Odessos] lives the Thracian tribe named Crobises." This is also evidenced by various ceramic pottery, made by hand or by a [Potter's wheel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potter's_wheel "Potter's wheel"), bronze ornaments for horse-fittings, and iron weapons, all found in Thracian necropolises dated 6th–4th c. BC near the villages of Dobrina, Kipra, Brestak, and others, all in [Varna Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna_Province "Varna Province"). The Thracians in the region were ruled by kings, who entered into unions with the [Odrysian kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysian_kingdom "Odrysian kingdom"), [Getae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getae "Getae"), or [Sapaeans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapaeans "Sapaeans")—large Thracian states existing between the 5th and 1st century BC. Between 336 and 280 BC, these Thracian states, along with Odessos, were conquered by [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great").

Archaeological findings have indicated that the population of northeast Thrace was very diverse, including the region around Odessos. Between the 6th century BC and the 4th century BC, the region was populated by [Scythians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythians "Scythians") who normally inhabited the central [Eurasian Steppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurasian_Steppe "Eurasian Steppe") (South Russia and Ukraine) and partly the area south of the river Istros (the Thracian name for the lower [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube")). Characteristics of their culture, weapons, and bronze objects have been found all over the region. Scythian horse ornaments are produced in "animal style", which is very close to the Thracian style, a possible explanation for the frequent mixture of both folks in northeastern Thrace. Many bronze artefacts give testimony to such a process, for example, applications and front plates for horseheads, as well as moulds for such products in nearby and more distant settlements. Since the 4th century BC the region had been populated by more [Getae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getae "Getae"), which is a Thracian tribe that populated both shores around the [Danube Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube_Delta "Danube Delta").

The [Celts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts") started populating the region after they invaded the [Balkan peninsula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkan_peninsula "Balkan peninsula") in 280 BC. Throughout northeast Bulgaria and even near Odessos, a significant number of bronze items with Celtic ornaments and typical weapons were discovered, all quickly adopted by Thracians. Arkovna, 80 km near Odessos, was probably the permanent capital of the Celts' last king Kavar (270/260–216/210 BC). Probably after the downfall of his kingdom, Celts blended with the greatly numbered Thracians in the country. Between the 2nd–1st c. BC in the present [Dobrudja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobruja "Dobruja") land, between Dyonissopolis ([Balchik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balchik "Balchik")) and Odessos, many small Scythian states were established. Their "kings" minted their coins in [mints](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mint_(facility) "Mint (facility)") located in cities on the western Black Sea coast, including Odessos.

The Thracians in northeast Thrace seem to be underdeveloped compared to their counterparts in South Thrace. The people lived in two types of settlements: non-fortified, located in fertile lands near water sources, and stone-built fortresses in a hard-to-reach mountain environment, where the kings' residences were usually located. Thracians engaged in farming, wood processing, hunting, and fishing. Among their art crafts is metal processing—especially weapons, excelling processing of bronze, making of bracelets, rings, Thracian type of fibulas, horse ornaments, arrowheads. Local goldsmiths used gold and silver to produce typical Thracian plate armour, ceremonial ornaments for the horses of the kings and the aristocracy, as well as valuable [pateras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patera "Patera") and [ritons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhyton "Rhyton").

Despite ethnic diversity, numerous internal and external conflicts, and cultural differences, the populations of northeastern Bulgaria and the cities along the seashore have demonstrated stable tolerance to each other. Conservatism is easily noticed in ceramic items and in religion. The highest deity of all was the [Thracian horseman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracian_horseman "Thracian horseman"), who had different names and functions in different places. Water-related deities were honoured as well, such as [the Three Graces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charites "Charites") or the water [Nymphs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nymph "Nymph") and [Zalmoxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zalmoxis "Zalmoxis") by the [Getae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getae "Getae"). During the centuries, especially by the end of the [Hellenistic period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenistic_period "Hellenistic period") (2nd–1st c. BC), Thracians adopted the more elaborate Hellenistic culture, thus acting as an intermediate for the continental Thracians.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-9)

### Antiquity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Antiquity")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/96/Warna_ruiny.jpg/250px-Warna_ruiny.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Warna_ruiny.jpg)

**Odessos** or **Odessus** ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Ὀδησσός)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-16) is one of the oldest ancient settlements in Bulgaria. Its name appears as **Odesopolis** (Ὀδησόπολις) in the _[Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periplus\_of\_Pseudo-Scylax "Periplus of Pseudo-Scylax")_; and as Odyssos or Odyssus in the [Synecdemus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synecdemus "Synecdemus") and in [Procopius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Procopius "Procopius").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-DGRG-17) It was established in the second quarter of the sixth century BC (585–550 BC) by [Miletian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miletus "Miletus")[Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks "Greeks") on the site of a previous Thracian settlement.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-19) The Miletian founded an _apoikia_ (trading post) of Odessos towards the end of the 7th c. BC (the earliest Greek archaeological material is dated 600–575 BC), or, according to [Pseudo-Scymnus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudo-Scymnus "Pseudo-Scymnus")_,_ in the time of [Astyages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Astyages "Astyages") (here, usually 572–570 BC is suggested), within an earlier Thracian settlement. The name _Odessos_ could have been pre-Greek, arguably of [Carian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carian_language "Carian language") origin. It was the presiding member of the Pontic [Pentapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pentapolis "Pentapolis"), consisting of Odessos, [Tomi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constan%C8%9Ba "Constanța"), [Callatis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Callatis "Callatis"), [Mesembria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mesembria "Mesembria"), and [Apollonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sozopol "Sozopol").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-DGRG-17) Odessos was a mixed community—contact zone between the [Ionian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ionia "Ionia")[Greeks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greeks "Greeks") and the [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians") tribes ([Getae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getae "Getae"), [Krobyzoi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krobyzoi "Krobyzoi"), [Terizi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terizi_(Getae_tribe) "Terizi (Getae tribe)")) of the [hinterland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinterland "Hinterland"). Excavations at nearby Thracian sites have shown uninterrupted occupation from the 7th to the 4th century BC and close commercial relations with the colony. The Greek alphabet has been used for inscriptions in [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracian_language "Thracian language") since at least the 5th century BC.

See also: [Derzelas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derzelas "Derzelas")

Odessos was included in the assessment of the [Delian League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delian_League "Delian League") of 425 BC. In 339 BC, it was unsuccessfully besieged by [Philip II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Macedon "Philip II of Macedon") (priests of the Getae persuaded him to conclude a treaty) but surrendered to [Alexander the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_the_Great "Alexander the Great") in 335 BC, and was later ruled by his [diadochus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diadochi "Diadochi")[Lysimachus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysimachus "Lysimachus"), against whom it rebelled in 313 BC as part of a coalition with other Pontic cities and the Getae. Nevertheless, at the end of the 4th century BC, the city became one of the strongholds of Lysimachus. The city became very prosperous from this time due to strong sea trade with many of the Mediterranean states and cities, supported by a wide range of local products. Shortly after 108 BC, Odessos recognised the suzerainty of [Mithridates VI of Pontus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mithridates_VI_of_Pontus "Mithridates VI of Pontus").

The Roman city, _Odessus_, first included into the _Praefectura orae maritimae_ and then in 15 AD annexed to the province of [Moesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moesia "Moesia") (later _Moesia Inferior_), covered 47 hectares in present-day central Varna and had prominent public baths, [Thermae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Thermae_(Varna) "Roman Thermae (Varna)"), erected in the late 2nd century AD (so-called Large (North) Ancient Roman Thermae), now the largest Roman remains in Bulgaria (the building was 100 m (328.08 ft) wide, 70 m (229.66 ft) long, and 25 m (82.02 ft) high) and fourth-largest-known [Roman baths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thermae "Thermae") in Europe which testify to the importance of the city. There is also the Small (South) Ancient Roman Thermae from the 5th–6th century AD.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-20) Additionally, in 2019, archaeologists discovered ruins of a Roman thermae building from the 5th century AD.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-21)

Major athletic games were held every five years, possibly attended by [Gordian III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordian_III "Gordian III") in 238.

The main aqueduct of Odessos was recently discovered during rescue excavations[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-22) north of the defensive wall. The aqueduct was built in three construction periods between the 4th and the 6th centuries; in the 4th century, the aqueduct was constructed together with the city wall, then at the end of the 4th to early 5th centuries when a pipeline was laid inside the initial masonry aqueduct. Thirdly, in the 6th century, an additional pipeline was added parallel to the original west of it and entered the city through a reconstruction of the fortress wall. The city minted coins, both as an autonomous [polis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polis "Polis") and under the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") from [Trajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan "Trajan") to [Salonina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornelia_Salonina "Cornelia Salonina"), the wife of [Gallienus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallienus "Gallienus"), some of which survive.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-DGRG-17)

Odessos was an early [Christian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Christianity "Early Christianity") centre, as testified by ruins of twelve early basilicas,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-23) a [monophysite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monophysite "Monophysite") monastery, and indications that one of the [Seventy Disciples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventy_Disciples "Seventy Disciples"), [Ampliatus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ampliatus "Ampliatus"), a follower of [Saint Andrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Andrew "Saint Andrew") (who, according to the [Bulgarian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Orthodox_Church "Bulgarian Orthodox Church") legend, preached in the city in 56 AD), served as bishop there. In 6th-century imperial documents, it was referred to as "holiest city," _sacratissima civitas_. In 442, a peace treaty was signed between [Theodosius II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_II "Theodosius II") and [Attila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attila "Attila") at Odessos. Furthermore, in 513, the city became a focal point of the [Vitalian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitalian_(general) "Vitalian (general)") revolt. Additionally, in 536, Emperor [Justinian I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I "Justinian I") designated it as the seat of the [Quaestura exercitus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaestura_exercitus "Quaestura exercitus") province ruled by a _prefect of Scythia_ or _quaestor Justinianus_ and including Lower Moesia, [Scythia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scythia "Scythia"), Caria, the [Aegean Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_Islands "Aegean Islands"), and Cyprus; later, the military camp outside Odessos was the seat of another senior Roman commander, _magister militum per Thracias_.

### Bulgarian conquest

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Bulgarian conquest")]

It has been suggested that the 681 AD peace treaty with the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") that established the new Bulgarian state was concluded at Varna and the first Bulgarian capital south of the Danube may have been provisionally located in its vicinity—possibly in an ancient city near Lake Varna's north shore named Theodorias (Θεοδωριάς) by Justinian I—before it moved to [Pliska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliska "Pliska")70 kilometres (43 miles) to the west.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-24)[Asparukh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asparuh_of_Bulgaria "Asparuh of Bulgaria") fortified the Varna river lowland by a [rampart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rampart_(fortification) "Rampart (fortification)") against a possible Byzantine landing; the _Asparuhov val_ (Asparukh's Wall) is still standing. Numerous 7th-century [Bulgar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgars "Bulgars") settlements have been excavated across the city and further west; the Varna lakes north shores, of all regions, were arguably most densely populated by Bulgars. It has been suggested that Asparukh was aware of the importance of the Roman military camp (_campus tribunalis_) established by Justinian I outside Odessos and considered it (or its remnants) as the legitimate seat of power for both Lower Moesia and Scythia.

### Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Middle Ages")]

During the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), the control over the city passed from Byzantine to Bulgarian hands several times. In the late 9th and the first half of the 10th century, Varna was the site of a principal [scriptorium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scriptorium "Scriptorium") of the [Preslav Literary School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preslav_Literary_School "Preslav Literary School") at a monastery endowed by Bulgarian ruler [Boris I of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_I_of_Bulgaria "Boris I of Bulgaria"), who may have also used it as his monastic retreat. The scriptorium may have played a key role in the development of the [Cyrillic script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyrillic_script "Cyrillic script") by Bulgarian scholars under the guidance of one of Saint [Cyril and Methodius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyril_and_Methodius "Cyril and Methodius")' disciples. [Karel Škorpil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karel_%C5%A0korpil "Karel Škorpil") suggested that Boris I may have been interred there. The synthetic culture with Hellenistic Thracian, Roman, as well as eastern—Armenian, Syrian, Persian—traits that developed around Odessos in the 6th century under Justinian I, may have influenced the Pliska-Preslav culture of the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire"), ostensibly in architecture and plastic decorative arts, but possibly also in literature, including Cyrillic scholarship. In 1201, [Kaloyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaloyan "Kaloyan") took over the Varna fortress, then in Byzantine hands, on [Holy Saturday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Saturday "Holy Saturday") using a [siege tower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_tower "Siege tower"), and secured it for the [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire").

See also: [Siege of Varna (1201)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Varna_(1201) "Siege of Varna (1201)")

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Varna_fortress.png/500px-Varna_fortress.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Varna_fortress.png)

Plan of Varna's medieval fortress.

By the late 13th century, with the 1261' [Treaty of Nymphaeum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Nymphaeum_(1261) "Treaty of Nymphaeum (1261)"), the offensive-defensive alliance between [Michael VIII Palaiologos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_VIII_Palaiologos "Michael VIII Palaiologos") and [Genoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Genoa "Republic of Genoa") was established, which opened up the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea") to Genoese commerce, eventually turning Varna into a thriving commercial port city frequented by Genoese and later also by [Venetian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Venice "Republic of Venice") and [Ragusan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ragusa "Republic of Ragusa") merchant ships. The first two maritime republics established their consulates, alongside their expatriate colonies in Varna (Ragusan merchants remained active at the port through the 17th century operating from their colony in nearby [Provadia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provadia "Provadia")). The city was flanked by two fortresses with smaller commercial ports of their own, Kastritsi and Galata, within sight of each other, and was protected by two other strongholds overlooking the lakes, Maglizh and Petrich. Wheat, animal skins, honey, wax, wine, timber, and other local agricultural produce for the Italian and Constantinople markets were the chief exports, and Mediterranean foods and luxury items were imported. The city introduced its own monetary standard, the _Varna [perper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperpyron "Hyperpyron")_, by the mid-14th century; the Bulgarian and Venetian currency exchange rate was fixed by a treaty. Fine jewellery, household ceramics, fine leather, and food processing, as well as other crafts, flourished; shipbuilding developed in the [Kamchiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kamchiya "Kamchiya") river mouth.

Fourteenth-century Italian [portolan charts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portolan_chart "Portolan chart") portrayed Varna as arguably the most important seaport between [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople "Constantinople") and the Danube delta; they usually labeled the region [Zagora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zagore_(region) "Zagore (region)"). The city was unsuccessfully besieged by [Amadeus VI, Count of Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amadeus_VI,_Count_of_Savoy "Amadeus VI, Count of Savoy"), who had captured all Bulgarian fortresses to the south of it, including Galata, in 1366. In 1386, Varna briefly became the capital of the spinoff [Despotate of Dobruja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Despotate_of_Dobruja "Despotate of Dobruja"), then was conquered by the [Ottoman Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") in 1389 (and again in 1444), ceded temporarily to [Manuel II Palaeologus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_II_Palaiologos "Manuel II Palaiologos") in 1413 (perhaps until 1444), and was sacked by [Tatars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_Tatars "Crimean Tatars") in 1414.

### Battle of Varna

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Battle of Varna")]

Main article: [Battle of Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Varna "Battle of Varna")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/39/VarnaMemorial.jpg/250px-VarnaMemorial.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:VarnaMemorial.jpg)

Memorial of the [Battle of Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Varna "Battle of Varna") of 1444 carved into an ancient [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians")[burial mound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tumulus "Tumulus")

On 10 November 1444, one of the last major battles of the [Crusades](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusade "Crusade") in European history was fought outside the city walls. The [Ottomans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Army "Ottoman Army") routed an army of 20,000–30,000 crusaders,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-25) commanded by [Władysław III of Poland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/W%C5%82adys%C5%82aw_III_of_Poland "Władysław III of Poland"), also Ulászló I of [Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hungary "Hungary") and [John Hunyadi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Hunyadi "John Hunyadi"), which had assembled at the port to set sail for Constantinople. The Christian army was attacked by a superior force of 55,000 or 60,000 Ottomans led by [Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultan "Sultan")[Murad II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murad_II "Murad II"). Ladislaus III was killed in a bold attempt to capture the sultan, earning the sobriquet _Warneńczyk_ (_of Varna_ in Polish; he is also known as _Várnai Ulászló_ in Hungarian or _Ladislaus Varnensis_ in Latin). The failure of the [Crusade of Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusade_of_Varna "Crusade of Varna") made the fall of Constantinople to the Ottomans in 1453 all but inevitable, and Varna (with all of Bulgaria) was to remain under Ottoman domination for over four centuries. Today, there is a [cenotaph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cenotaph "Cenotaph") of Ladislaus III in Varna.

### Late Ottoman rule

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Varna,_Bulgaria&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Late Ottoman rule")]

A major port, agricultural, trade, and shipbuilding centre for the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") in the 16th and 17th centuries, preserving a significant and economically active Bulgarian population, Varna was later made one of the _Quadrilateral Fortresses_ (along with [Rousse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rousse "Rousse"), [Shumen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shumen "Shumen"), and [Silistra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silistra "Silistra")), severing [Dobruja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dobruja "Dobruja") from the rest of Bulgaria and containing Russia in the [Russo-Turkish wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Russo-Turkish_wars "History of the Russo-Turkish wars"). The Russians [stormed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Storming_of_Varna_(1773) "Storming of Varna (1773)") the city in 1773 and [besieged](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Varna_(1828) "Siege of Varna (1828)") it in 1828; however, both ended in failure.

See also: [Siege of Varna (1828)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Varna_(1828) "Siege of Varna (1828)")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Etnografisch_Museum.jpg/250px-Etnografisch_Museum.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Etnografisch_Museum.jpg)

Ottoman period townhouse

In the early 19th century, many local Greeks joined the patriotic organisation [Filiki Eteria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filiki_Eteria "Filiki Eteria"). At the outbreak of the [Greek War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_War_of_Independence "Greek War of Independence") (1821), revolutionary activity was recorded in Varna. As a result, local notables who participated in the Greek national movement were executed by the Ottoman authorities, while others managed to escape to Greece, where they continued their struggle for independence.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria#cite_note-26)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a9/1877-11-30%2C_La_Ilustraci%C3%B3n_Espa%C3%B1ola_y_Americana%2C_Cr%C3%B3nica_ilustrada_de_la_Guerra_de_Oriente_%28cropped%29_Vista_general_de_Varna%2C_tomada_desde_el_mar.jpg/250px-1877-11-30%2C_La_Ilustraci%C3%B3n_Espa%C3%B1ola_y_Americana%2C_Cr%C3%B3nica_ilustrada_de_la_Guerra_de_Oriente_%28cropped%29_Vista_general_de_Varna%2C_tomada_desde_el_mar.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:1877-11-30,_La_Ilustraci%C3%B3n_Espa%C3%B1ola_y_Americana,_Cr%C3%B3nica_ilustrada_de_la_Guerra_de_Oriente_(cropped)_Vista_general_de_Varna,_tomada_desde_el_mar.jpg)

Varna during the late Ottoman rule

The British and French, campaigning against Russia in the [Crimean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crimean_War "Crimean War") (1854–1856), used Varna as headquarters and principal naval base; many soldiers died of cholera, and the city was devastated by a fire. A British and a French monument mark the cemeteries where cholera victims were interred. In 1866, the first railroad in Bulgaria established a connection between Varna and [Rousse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruse,_Bulgaria "Ruse, Bulgaria") on the Danube, linking the Ottoman capital [Constantinople](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul") with Central Europe; for a few years, the [Orient Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orient_Express "Orient Express") ran through that route. The port of Varna developed as a major supplier of food—notably wheat from the adjacent breadbasket [Southern Dobruja](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Dobruja "Southern Dobruja")—to Constantinople and a busy hub for European imports to the capital; 12 foreign consulates opened in the city. Local Bulgarians took part in the [National Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_National_Revival "Bulgarian National Revival"); [Vasil Levski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasil_Levski "Vasil Levski") established a secret revolutionary committee.

**Burgas** ([Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_language "Bulgarian language"): Бургас, pronounced[[burˈɡas]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Bulgarian "Help:IPA/Bulgarian")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/9/94/LL-Q7918_%28bul%29-Kiril_kovachev-%D0%91%D1%83%D1%80%D0%B3%D0%B0%D1%81.wav/LL-Q7918_%28bul%29-Kiril_kovachev-%D0%91%D1%83%D1%80%D0%B3%D0%B0%D1%81.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q7918_(bul)-Kiril_kovachev-%D0%91%D1%83%D1%80%D0%B3%D0%B0%D1%81.wav "File:LL-Q7918 (bul)-Kiril kovachev-Бургас.wav")), sometimes transliterated as **Bourgas**, is the second largest city on the [Bulgarian Black Sea Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Black_Sea_Coast "Bulgarian Black Sea Coast") in the region of [Northern Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Thrace "Northern Thrace") and the [fourth-largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bulgaria "List of cities and towns in Bulgaria") in [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria") after [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia"), [Plovdiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv "Plovdiv"), and [Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Varna,_Bulgaria "Varna, Bulgaria"), with a population of 210,382 inhabitants, while 225,945 live in its urban area. It is the capital of [Burgas Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas_Province "Burgas Province") and an important industrial, transport, cultural and tourist centre.

The city is surrounded by the [Burgas Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas_Lakes "Burgas Lakes") and located at the westernmost point of the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea"), at the large [Burgas Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas_Bay "Burgas Bay"). [LUKOIL Neftochim Burgas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LUKOIL_Neftochim_Burgas "LUKOIL Neftochim Burgas") is the largest [oil refinery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_refinery "Oil refinery") in southeastern Europe and the largest industrial enterprise. The [Port of Burgas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Burgas "Port of Burgas") is the second largest port in Bulgaria, and [Burgas Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas_Airport "Burgas Airport") is the second most important in the country. Burgas is the centre of the Bulgarian fishing and fish processing industry.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-USNI-2)

## Names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Names")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Burgas_Bulgaria_by_Sentinel-2_20190831.jpg/250px-Burgas_Bulgaria_by_Sentinel-2_20190831.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burgas_Bulgaria_by_Sentinel-2_20190831.jpg)

Burgas as seen from space

The city's name is considered to go back to the Greek word for "tower", "_Pyrgos_" ([Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language"): Πύργος). It is mentioned by the Byzantine poet [Manuel Philes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Philes "Manuel Philes") and rendered in Turkish as _Burgaz_. There are several alternative explanations for the name's origin. One of them states the city's name comes from [Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gothic_language "Gothic language") name "baurgs", meaning "signified consolidated [walled](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_wall "Defensive wall") villages".[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-3) According to Bulgarian prof. Kiril Vlahov, the name of the city comes from the [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracian_language "Thracian language") word "_pyurg_", meaning "fortification of wooden beams".

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

### Topography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Topography")]

Burgas is situated at the westernmost point of the bay by the same name and in the eastern part of the [Burgas Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas_Plain?action=edit&redlink=1 "Burgas Plain (page does not exist)"), in the east of the [Upper Thracian Plain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Thracian_Plain "Upper Thracian Plain"). Burgas is located some 360 kilometres (224 mi) from Sofia, 255 km (158 mi) from Plovdiv, 130 km (81 mi) from Varna, and 332 km (206 mi) from [Istanbul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul "Istanbul"). To the west, south and north, the city is surrounded by the [Burgas Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas_Lakes "Burgas Lakes"): [Burgas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Burgas "Lake Burgas"), [Atanasovsko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Atanasovsko "Lake Atanasovsko"), and [Mandrensko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Mandrensko "Lake Mandrensko"), which are home to several hundred bird species. [Pan-European corridor 8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-European_corridors "Pan-European corridors") passes through the city,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-4) the [European routes E87](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_route_E87 "European route E87") and [E773](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_route_E773 "European route E773"), and the longest national rout I/6. The [St. Anastasia Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Anastasia_Island "St. Anastasia Island") is a part of the city.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-5)

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Climate")]

Under the [Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"), Burgas has a [humid subtropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") (Köppen: _Cfa_). The summertime in Burgas lasts about five months from mid-May until late September. Average temperatures during high season is 24°C (75°F). Summertime sea temperatures stay around 23–24°C (73–75°F) at sunrise and go up to 29–30°C (84–86°F) by dusk, averaging 26°C (79°F). Winters are milder compared with the inland part of the country, with average temperatures of 4–5°C (39–41°F) and below 0°C (32°F) during the night. Snow is possible in December, January, February and rarely in March; however, it can quickly melt. The highest temperature was recorded in June 2007, at 42.8°C (109°F) and the lowest at −21.6°C (−7°F) in January 1942.

### Flora and fauna

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Flora and fauna")]

The [Burgas Wetlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas_Wetlands "Burgas Wetlands") are highly recognized for their significance to biodiversity and as a resource pool for products used by people.

Lake Burgas is Bulgaria's largest lake and is in the middle of the city. It is important for migrating birds. Over 250 species of birds inhabit the lake area, 61 of which are endangered in Bulgaria and 9 globally, attracting keen birdwatchers from all over the world. The lakes are also home to important fish and [invertebrates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invertebrate "Invertebrate"). In the site have been recorded several [IUCN Red-Listed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IUCN_Red_List "IUCN Red List") species of animals – 5 invertebrates, 4 fish, 4 [amphibians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphibian "Amphibian"), 3 [reptiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reptiles "Reptiles"), 5 birds and 3 [mammals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mammal "Mammal"). Situated along the second largest migration path of birds in Europe, the [Via Pontica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Pontica "Via Pontica"), the site is an important stopover and staging site for a large number of water-birds, raptors and passerines. Yearly during migration and wintering more than 20,000 (up to 100,000) waterbirds congregate there.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-Ramsar_Convention-9)

The Atanasovo Lake is one of two salt-water lakes in the Black Sea region and contains rare and representative examples of wetland habitats. It is a hot spot for biodiversity, with many Red-Listed species of plants and animals. It is a well-known bottleneck site for migratory birds, with around 60,000 raptors and 240,000 storks, pelicans and cranes passing over the site and often landing in large numbers for staging. The highest numbers in Europe of migrating [Great white pelican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_white_pelican "Great white pelican") (_Pelecanus onocrotalus_), [Dalmatian pelican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalmatian_pelican "Dalmatian pelican") (_Pelecanus crispus_), [Western marsh harrier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_marsh_harrier "Western marsh harrier") (_Circus aeruginosus_) and [Red-footed Falcon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red-footed_Falcon "Red-footed Falcon") (_Falco vespertinus_) have been recorded here.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-Ramsar_Convention-9)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c6/Bronze-Alexander_Severus-Deultum_AE25_Moushmov_3583.jpg/250px-Bronze-Alexander_Severus-Deultum_AE25_Moushmov_3583.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bronze-Alexander_Severus-Deultum_AE25_Moushmov_3583.jpg)

[Alexander Severus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Severus "Alexander Severus") coin from the _Colonia Flavia Pacis Deultensium_

The earliest signs of life in the region date back 3,000 years, to the [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age "Bronze Age") and the early [Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age "Iron Age"). The favorable conditions on the fertile plain, around the sea, have brought people here from early antiquity. The biggest mark was left by the Thracians who made the region rich in archaeological finds (from around 4th c. BC). This includes their sanctuary at [Beglik Tash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beglik_Tash "Beglik Tash") along the south coast and a burial mound near [Sunny Beach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunny_Beach "Sunny Beach"). They built the mineral baths of [Aquae Calidae](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquae_Calidae,_Bulgaria "Aquae Calidae, Bulgaria") and the fortress _Tyrsis_.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-municipality-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-pocket-11) Under [Darius I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Darius_I "Darius I"), it became part of the [Achaemenid Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire "Achaemenid Empire"), before the [Odrysian kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysian_kingdom "Odrysian kingdom") was established. Greeks from [Apollonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sozopol "Sozopol") built a marketplace to trade with the Thracians, in what is now the neighborhood of [Pobeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pobeda,_Burgas "Pobeda, Burgas").

During the rule of the [Ancient Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Rome "Ancient Rome"), near Burgas, [_Colonia Flavia Pacis Deultensium_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Develtos "Develtos") (_Deultum_, _Dibaltum_, or _Develtum_) was established as a military colony for veterans by [Vespasian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vespasian "Vespasian") in AD 70. The Romans built this _colonia_ on the main road [Via Pontica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Pontica "Via Pontica"). It was the second most important city in the province [Haemimontus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haemimontus "Haemimontus").

In 376 the Goths destroyed an elite Roman [company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_(military_unit) "Company (military unit)") near Develtum at the [Battle of Dibaltum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Dibaltum "Battle of Dibaltum").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-12)

### Bulgarian and Byzantine Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Bulgarian and Byzantine Middle Ages")]

In the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), there were important settlements in the area: the fortress _Skafida_, _Poros_, _Rusokastron_ ([Battle of Rusokastro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Rusokastro "Battle of Rusokastro")), the Baths called Aquae Calidae and used by Byzantine, Bulgarian and Ottoman Emperors; a small fortress called _Pyrgos_ was erected where Burgas is today and was most probably used as a watchtower. Under the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") it became an important city on the [Black Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea") coast. The Bulgarian ruler [Krum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krum "Krum") built the [Erkesiya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erkesiya?action=edit&redlink=1 "Erkesiya (page does not exist)"), a 140 km (87 mi)-long border wall from the Black Sea (near Gorno Ezerovo) to the [Maritsa River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritsa_River "Maritsa River").

In 1206, the [Latin Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Empire "Latin Empire")[Henry of Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_of_Flanders "Henry of Flanders") (see [Fourth Crusade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade "Fourth Crusade")) destroyed Aquae Calidae, which was known as Thermopolis at this time, The baths were later rebuilt by the Byzantines and Bulgarians. Poros was mentioned in a 1270 document of the Patriarchate of Constantinople.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-IW6065-13) Close to Poros took place the [Battle of Skafida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Skafida "Battle of Skafida") in 1304, when the Bulgarian Tsar [Todor Svetoslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodore_Svetoslav_of_Bulgaria "Theodore Svetoslav of Bulgaria") defeated the Byzantines and conquered the southern Black Sea coast.

At the beginning of the 14th century, the region was sacked by the [Catalan Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catalan_Company "Catalan Company"). In the 13th century Burgas is mentioned by the Byzantine poet [Manuel Philes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manuel_Philes "Manuel Philes") in his works as _Burgas_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-IW6065-13)

### Ottoman rule

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Ottoman rule")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7e/Illustration_from_Views_in_the_Ottoman_Dominions_by_Luigi_Mayer%2C_digitally_enhanced_by_rawpixel-com_12.jpg/250px-Illustration_from_Views_in_the_Ottoman_Dominions_by_Luigi_Mayer%2C_digitally_enhanced_by_rawpixel-com_12.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Illustration_from_Views_in_the_Ottoman_Dominions_by_Luigi_Mayer,_digitally_enhanced_by_rawpixel-com_12.jpg)

Burgas in [Ottoman Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Bulgaria "Ottoman Bulgaria"), painted by [Luigi Mayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luigi_Mayer "Luigi Mayer")

Like many of the towns surrounding it, Burgas was conquered by the Ottomans with the rest of Bulgaria in the late 14th century, only to be [returned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Gallipoli "Treaty of Gallipoli") to the Byzantine Empire during the [Ottoman Interregnum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Interregnum "Ottoman Interregnum") and retained by the Byzantines until the fall of the Empire to the Ottomans in 1453. It was only in the 17th century that a settlement renamed to _Ahelo-Pirgas_ grew in the modern area of the city. It was later renamed to _Burgas_ again and had only about 3,000 inhabitants. In the early 19th century Burgas was depopulated after raids by _kurzdhali_ bandits. By the mid-19th century it had recovered its economic prominence through the growth of craftsmanship and the export of grain.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-14) The city was a small town in [İslimye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliven "Sliven") (Sliven) sanjak in at first [Rumelia Eyalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumelia_Eyalet "Rumelia Eyalet"), after that in the [Silistra Eyalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silistra_Eyalet "Silistra Eyalet") and [Edirne Eyalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edirne_Eyalet "Edirne Eyalet") before the liberation in 1878.

In the 17th and 18th centuries Burgas became an important port for [cereal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cereal "Cereal") and possesses its own grain measure, the _Burgas-Kile_. The town was the regional centre of trade and administrative centre of the Burgas Kaaza.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-15)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-17)

In 1865 the port of Burgas was after [Trapezunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trabzon "Trabzon") the second most important Ottoman port in the Black Sea. Burgas was at this time the major centre on the southern [Bulgarian Black Sea Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Black_Sea_Coast "Bulgarian Black Sea Coast").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-19)

### From liberation to 1945

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: From liberation to 1945")]

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/25/Burgas-alexandrovska-street-1906.jpg/250px-Burgas-alexandrovska-street-1906.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burgas-alexandrovska-street-1906.jpg)

Alexandrovska Street in 1906

It was a department centre in [Eastern Rumelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Rumelia "Eastern Rumelia") before incorporated in the [Principality of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Bulgaria "Principality of Bulgaria") in 1885. From the late 19th century Burgas became an important economic and industry center. The first development plan of the city was adopted in 1891 and the city's layout and appearance changed, especially through the newly constructed public buildings.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-RMB-20) In 1888, the city library was founded, in 1891 the sea garden was created and in 1897 the Cathedral of the Holy brothers Cyril and Methodius was built. In 1895 Georgi Ivanov opened the first Printing house in Burgas, followed by the house of _Christo Velchev_ in 1897, which changed in 1900 his name in _Velchevi Brothers Printing house_.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-IK220-21)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/Burgas_Plan_1913.jpg/250px-Burgas_Plan_1913.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Burgas_Plan_1913.jpg)

A 1913 plan of the city

The opening of the railway line to Plovdiv on 27 May 1890 and the deep water port in 1903 were important stages of this boom and led to the rapid industrialization of the city.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-23) In the period after 151 factories were founded. Among them were the _Sugar refinery_ founded by [Avram Chaliovski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Avram_Chaliovski?action=edit&redlink=1 "Avram Chaliovski (page does not exist)"), the _Great Bulgarian Mills_ of [Ivan Chadzipetrov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Chadzipetrov?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ivan Chadzipetrov (page does not exist)") and the oil and soap factory _Kambana_.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-RMB-20) In 1900 the mineral springs by the ancient Aquae Calidae were included in the urban area. In 1903, the new building of the [Burgas Central railway station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas_Central_railway_station "Burgas Central railway station") opened.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-IW210-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-25)

Founded in 1924 in Burgas _Deweko_ (now HemusMark AD) was the first pencil factory in Southeastern Europe and became in 1937 official supplier to the Bulgarian Monarchy.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-26) 1925 opened in Burgas a specialized high school for mechanics and technologies. The following year, a large covered market was opened.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-RMB-20) Because of the cold wave in winter 1928/29 the Black Sea iced in late January and early February, so that the island of Sveta Anastasia could be reached on foot.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-27) 1934, Burgas already had 34,260 inhabitants.

### Communism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Communism")]

During World War II on 9 September 1944 Red Army troops occupied the city and soon the whole country.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-28) In the following [People's Courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Court_(Bulgaria) "People's Court (Bulgaria)"), especially members of the wealthy families of the intelligentsia and members of the [Bar Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bar_Association "Bar Association") were convicted. The two Chambers of the People's Courts met in Burgas in the former building of the Chamber of Commerce and Industry of Burgas (now the seat of the Governor of the Province Burgas).[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-IW250-29)

After the Communists took power in 1945, the German and Italian School and the People's University were closed[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-Burneva/Murdsheva-30) and over 160 factories and businesses (including the large companies _Great Bulgarian Mills_, _Veriga_, _Plug_, _Dab_, etc.), shops, baths and other private property were nationalized. The [nationalization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalization "Nationalization") and inability to lead by the new rulers led the companies to the collapse of the food supply and the shortage of goods of daily life in the city.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-IW250-29) The political repression against the population of Burgas continued for the next few years. Access to universities and other higher education in the Bulgarian capital was refused for the young people of Burgas and some of them were interned in [prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prison "Prison") and [labor camps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forced_labour_camps_in_Communist_Bulgaria "Forced labour camps in Communist Bulgaria").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-IW250-29)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Neftochim-vaya-dinev_cropped.jpg/250px-Neftochim-vaya-dinev_cropped.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Neftochim-vaya-dinev_cropped.jpg)

The [Neftohim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LUKOIL_Neftochim_Burgas "LUKOIL Neftochim Burgas") refinery, one of the major Bulgarian industrial capacities, built during the Socialist era

After the end of the Second World War, the [Haganah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haganah "Haganah") organised several convoys for the European survivors of the [Holocaust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Holocaust "The Holocaust"), which departed on ships from Burgas for Palestine. These convoys allowed 12,000 people, including the Jewish population of the city, to emigrate.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-32) In the following years the city center of Burgas, unlike many other Bulgarian cities, was not much affected by Communist-type urbanization and has kept much of its 19th- and early-20th-century architecture. A number of oil and chemical companies were gradually built.

The terrorists of the [2 June Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2_June_Movement "2 June Movement"), Till Meyer, [Gabriele Rollnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabriele_Rollnik "Gabriele Rollnik"), Gudrun Stürmer and Angelika Goder were arrested on 21 June 1978 in Burgas by West German officials and then brought into the [Federal Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Republic_of_Germany "Federal Republic of Germany").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-33)

### Post 1990

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Post 1990")]

Today the local port is the largest in Bulgaria adding significantly to the regional economy. Burgas also hosts annual national exhibitions and international festivals and has a vibrant student population of over 6,000 that add to the city's appeal. The historical society also maintains open-air museums at [Beglik Tash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beglik_Tash "Beglik Tash") and [Develtum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Develtum "Develtum").

Several countries have General Consulates in Burgas, among them [Belarus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belarus "Belarus"), [Czech Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Czech_Republic "Czech Republic"), [Estonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estonia "Estonia"), [Georgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(country) "Georgia (country)"),[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-34)[Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece "Greece"), [Romania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romania "Romania"), [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia"), [Sierra Leone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sierra_Leone "Sierra Leone"),[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-35)[Turkey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey "Turkey") and [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-36)

In 2023 Bulgaria took back the concession it had granted to Lukoil in 2011 to run the Rosenets oil terminal.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-37)

#### 2012 bus bombing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Burgas&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: 2012 bus bombing")]

Main article: [2012 Burgas bus bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Burgas_bus_bombing "2012 Burgas bus bombing")

On 18 July 2012 a terrorist attack was carried out by a [suicide bomber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_bomber "Suicide bomber")[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-38) on a passenger bus transporting Israeli tourists at the Burgas Airport. The bus was carrying forty-two Israelis, mainly youths, from the airport to their hotels, after arriving on a flight from [Tel Aviv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tel_Aviv "Tel Aviv"). The explosion killed the Bulgarian bus driver and five Israelis.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgas#cite_note-haaretznames19j-39)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0f/Bulgaria-CIA_WFB_Map.png/250px-Bulgaria-CIA_WFB_Map.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bulgaria-CIA_WFB_Map.png)

Map of Bulgaria

This is a complete **list of all cities in Bulgaria** sorted by population. Province capitals are shown in **bold**. Primary sources are the [National Statistical Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Statistical_Institute_(Bulgaria) "National Statistical Institute (Bulgaria)") (NSI)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bulgaria#cite_note-census2011-1) and the [Bulgarian Academy of Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Academy_of_Sciences "Bulgarian Academy of Sciences").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bulgaria#cite_note-BAN-2)

The largest city is Sofia, with about 1.4 million inhabitants, and the smallest is [Melnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melnik,_Bulgaria "Melnik, Bulgaria"), with about 300. Towns are not necessarily larger than all villages. Indeed, many villages are more populous than many towns – compare for instance [Lozen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lozen,_Sofia_Province "Lozen, Sofia Province"), a large village with more than 6,000 inhabitants, with Melnik.

The **[Ivan Vazov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Vazov "Ivan Vazov") National Theatre** ([Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_language "Bulgarian language"): Народен театър „Иван Вазов“, _\_Naroden teatar „Ivan Vazov“\__) is [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria")'s national theatre, as well as the oldest and most authoritative theatre in the country and one of the important landmarks of [Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia "Sofia"), the capital of Bulgaria. It is located in the centre of the city, with the facade facing the [City Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Garden_(Sofia) "City Garden (Sofia)").

The Ivan Vazov National Theatre has a well-equipped main stage with 750 seats, a smaller 120-seat stage and an additional 70-seat one on the fourth floor. The theatre has been host to productions from notable theatre directors such as [Alexander Morfov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Morfov "Alexander Morfov") who has been the Chief director since 1993.

The building's facade is depicted on the [obverse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obverse_and_reverse "Obverse and reverse") of the Bulgarian 50 [levs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_lev "Bulgarian lev") banknote, issued in 1999 and 2006.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Vazov_National_Theatre#cite_note-1)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ivan_Vazov_National_Theatre&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Founded in 1904 by the artists from the _\_Salza i Smyah\__ company, the theatre was initially called simply the National Theatre, but before being named after the prominent writer Ivan Vazov it also bore the name of [Krastyu Sarafov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krastyu_Sarafov?action=edit&redlink=1 "Krastyu Sarafov (page does not exist)") between 1952 and 1962. Vazov's play _[The Outcasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Outcasts\_(play) "The Outcasts (play)")_ was the first to be performed at the theatre when it opened. The theatre's [neoclassical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassical_architecture "Neoclassical architecture") building, designed by famous [Viennese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna") theatre architects [Hermann Helmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hermann_Helmer "Hermann Helmer") and [Ferdinand Fellner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Fellner "Ferdinand Fellner"), was finished in 1906 and opened on 3 January 1907.

A theatrical school was established as part of the National Theatre in 1925. The building was extensively damaged by a fire in 1923 during an anniversary celebration, but was reconstructed in 1929 by German architect [Martin Dülfer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_D%C3%BClfer "Martin Dülfer"). The [bombing of Sofia in World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Sofia_in_World_War_II "Bombing of Sofia in World War II") caused further damage to the building, but it was reconstructed in 1945. Another reconstruction followed in 1971–1975, and a [€](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euro "Euro")100,000 restoration project was implemented in 2006.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Vazov_National_Theatre#cite_note-2)

### **Ivan Vazov National Theatre**

The **Ivan Vazov National Theatre** is Bulgaria's oldest and most authoritative theatre, named after the famous Bulgarian writer Ivan Vazov. Established in 1904, it is a prime example of Neo-Baroque architecture and a cultural landmark in Sofia. The theatre's grand facade, adorned with sculptures and intricate details, makes it a must-see during a Culture and History tour of the city.

### History & Origins

The theatre was designed by the Viennese architects Hermann Helmer and Ferdinand Fellner, who were renowned for their work on European theatres. Construction began in 1904 and was completed in 1907. The building survived a fire in 1923 and was restored to its original grandeur. It has since hosted countless performances, cementing its place as a cultural hub.

During World War II, the theatre was damaged but later restored. It continues to be a symbol of Bulgarian resilience and artistic excellence. The theatre's repertoire includes classical and contemporary plays, operas, and ballets, attracting both locals and tourists.

### Architecture & Features

The theatre's exterior features a grand portico with six columns, topped by a pediment with a sculptural group. The interior is equally impressive, with a lavish auditorium, ornate ceilings, and gold-leaf decorations. The stage is one of the largest in Bulgaria, equipped with modern technical facilities.

The building's facade is adorned with statues of Greek muses, adding to its artistic appeal. The theatre's main hall seats 750 spectators and is known for its excellent acoustics. The lobby features marble staircases and crystal chandeliers, reflecting the opulence of the early 20th century.

### Legends & Facts

1. The theatre's foundation stone was laid in 1904, but the building was not completed until 1907 due to financial difficulties.  
2. The fire of 1923 destroyed much of the interior, but the facade remained intact, allowing for a faithful restoration.  
3. The theatre was named after Ivan Vazov in 1925, honoring his contributions to Bulgarian literature.

### Tourist Tips

Visit the theatre during the day to admire its architecture, or attend an evening performance for a full cultural experience. The box office opens at 10 AM, and tickets can be purchased online or in person. Guided tours are available but must be booked in advance.

*   Alexander Nevsky Cathedral - A stunning Orthodox cathedral with golden domes and intricate mosaics.
*   Vitosha Boulevard - Sofia's main shopping street, lined with cafes and boutiques.
*   National Palace of Culture - A modern multipurpose venue hosting concerts and exhibitions.
*   Borisova Gradina - The city's oldest and largest park, perfect for a leisurely stroll.

### Practical FAQ for Travelers

#### What are the opening hours?

The theatre is open from 10 AM to 6 PM on weekdays and 10 AM to 2 PM on weekends.

#### What is the best time to visit?

Mornings are less crowded, but evenings offer the chance to see a performance.

#### How long does a visit take?

A self-guided tour takes about 30 minutes, while a performance lasts 2-3 hours.

#### Are photos allowed?

Yes, but flash photography is prohibited during performances.

#### Is the theatre accessible for kids?

Yes, but some performances may not be suitable for young children.

#### Is there a dress code?

Casual attire is acceptable for tours, but evening performances may require more formal wear.

**Sofia**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-19) is the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_city "Capital city") and [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_and_towns_in_Bulgaria "List of cities and towns in Bulgaria") of [Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria"). It is situated in the [Sofia Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Valley "Sofia Valley") at the foot of the [Vitosha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitosha "Vitosha") mountain, in the western part of the country. The city is built west of the [Iskar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iskar_(river) "Iskar (river)") river and has many mineral springs, such as the [Sofia Central Mineral Baths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Central_Mineral_Baths "Sofia Central Mineral Baths"). It has a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate").

Known as [Serdica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica "Serdica") in [antiquity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_antiquity "Classical antiquity"), Sofia has been an area of human habitation since at least 7000 BC. The recorded history of the city begins with the attestation of the conquest of Serdica by the [Roman Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Republic "Roman Republic") in 29 BC from the [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celtic_settlement_of_Southeast_Europe "Celtic settlement of Southeast Europe") tribe [Serdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdi "Serdi"). During the decline of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"), the city was raided by [Huns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns "Huns"), [Visigoths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visigoths "Visigoths"), [Avars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pannonian_Avars "Pannonian Avars"), and [Slavs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavs "Slavs"). In 809, Serdica was incorporated into the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire") by [Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khan_(title) "Khan (title)")[Krum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krum "Krum") and became known as Sredets. In 1018, the [Byzantines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") ended Bulgarian rule until 1194, when it was reincorporated by the [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire"). Sredets became a major administrative, economic, cultural and literary hub until its conquest by the [Ottomans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") in 1382. From 1530 to 1836, Sofia was the regional capital of [Rumelia Eyalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumelia_Eyalet "Rumelia Eyalet"), the Ottoman Empire's largest and most important province. Bulgarian rule was restored in 1878. Sofia was selected as the capital of the [Third Bulgarian State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Bulgaria "Principality of Bulgaria") in the next year, ushering a period of intense demographic and economic growth.

Sofia is the [14th-largest city in the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_in_the_European_Union_by_population_within_city_limits "List of cities in the European Union by population within city limits"). It is surrounded by mountains including Vitosha to the south, [Lyulin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyulin_Mountain "Lyulin Mountain") to the west, and the [Balkan Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkan_Mountains "Balkan Mountains") to the north. It is the [fourth highest European capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_capital_cities_by_elevation "List of capital cities by elevation") after [Andorra la Vella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andorra_la_Vella "Andorra la Vella"), [San Marino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Marino "San Marino") and [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid"). Sofia is home to several universities, cultural institutions and commercial companies. The city has been described as the "triangle of [religious tolerance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religious_tolerance "Religious tolerance")". This is because three temples of three major world religions—[Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity"), [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam "Islam") and [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism "Judaism")—are situated close together: [Sveta Nedelya Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Nedelya_Church "St Nedelya Church"), [Banya Bashi Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banya_Bashi_Mosque "Banya Bashi Mosque") and [Sofia Synagogue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Synagogue "Sofia Synagogue").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-20) This triangle was recently expanded to a "square" and includes the Catholic [Cathedral of St Joseph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathedral_of_St_Joseph,_Sofia "Cathedral of St Joseph, Sofia").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-21)

The [Boyana Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyana_Church "Boyana Church") in Sofia, constructed during the [Second Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire") and holding much patrimonial symbolism to the [Bulgarian Orthodox Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Orthodox_Church "Bulgarian Orthodox Church"), was included on the [World Heritage List](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") in 1979. With its cultural significance in [Southeast Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Europe "Southeast Europe"), Sofia is home to the [National Opera and Ballet of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Opera_and_Ballet_of_Bulgaria "National Opera and Ballet of Bulgaria"), the [National Palace of Culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Palace_of_Culture "National Palace of Culture"), the [Vasil Levski National Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasil_Levski_National_Stadium "Vasil Levski National Stadium"), the [Ivan Vazov National Theatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Vazov_National_Theatre "Ivan Vazov National Theatre"), the [National Archaeological Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Archaeological_Museum,_Bulgaria "National Archaeological Museum, Bulgaria"), and the [Serdica Amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre_of_Serdica "Amphitheatre of Serdica"). The [Museum of Socialist Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Socialist_Art,_Sofia "Museum of Socialist Art, Sofia") includes many sculptures and posters that educate visitors about the lifestyle in [communist Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Bulgaria "People's Republic of Bulgaria").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-22)

The population of Sofia declined from 70,000 in the late 18th century, through 19,000 in 1870, to 11,649 in 1878, after which it began increasing.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-isotriq-23) Sofia hosts some 1.28 million[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-population-10) residents within a territory of 500 km 2,[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-area_total-24) a concentration of 17.9% of the country's population within the 200th percentile of the country's territory.
