## Names

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Names")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ac/Sredets_seal_1878.jpg/250px-Sredets_seal_1878.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sredets_seal_1878.jpg)

The first seal of the city, from 1878, which calls it _Sredets,_ its name in [Old Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Church_Slavonic "Old Church Slavonic")

For a long time, the city possessed[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-constantine-28) the name, **Serdica** ([Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Σαρδική, _Serdikē_, or Σαρδική, _Sardikē_; [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language"): _Serdica_ or _Sardica_), derived from the tribe _[Serdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdi "Serdi")_, who were either of [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-britannica.com-17)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-tr-29)[Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts"),[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-The_Cambridge_Ancient_History_1992,_page_600-30) or mixed Thracian-Celtic origin.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-32) The emperor [Marcus Ulpius Traianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan "Trajan") (53–117 AD) gave the city the combinative name of _[Ulpia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ulpia\_gens "Ulpia gens") Serdica_;[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-world-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-books.google.bg-34) Ulpia may be derived from an Umbrian cognate of the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin") word _lupus_, meaning "wolf"[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-35) or from the Latin _vulpes_ (fox). It seems that the first written mention of _Serdica_ was made during his reign and the last mention was in the 19th century in a Bulgarian text (Сардакіи, _Sardaki_). Other names given to Sofia, such as **Serdonpolis** ([Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Greek_language "Byzantine Greek language")[Ancient Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greek_language "Ancient Greek language"): Σερδῶν πόλις, "City of the Serdi") and **Triaditza** (Τριάδιτζα, "Trinity"), were mentioned by [Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire")[Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language") sources or coins. The Slavic name **Sredets** ([Church Slavonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Slavonic_language "Church Slavonic language"): Срѣдецъ), which is related to "middle" (среда, "sreda") and to the city's earliest name, first appeared on paper in an 11th-century text. The city was called _Atralisa_ by the Arab traveller [Idrisi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_al-Idrisi "Muhammad al-Idrisi") and _Strelisa_, _Stralitsa_, or _Stralitsion_ by the [Crusaders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusaders "Crusaders").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-36)

The name _Sofia_ comes from the [Saint Sofia Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sofia_Church,_Sofia "Saint Sofia Church, Sofia"),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-37) as opposed to the prevailing [Slavic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavic_languages "Slavic languages")[origin of Bulgarian cities and towns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Bulgaria_province_name_etymologies "List of Bulgaria province name etymologies"). The origin is in the Greek word _[sophía](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophia\_(wisdom) "Sophia (wisdom)")_ (σοφία, "wisdom"). The earliest works where this latest name is registered are the duplicate of the Gospel of Serdica, in a dialogue between two salesmen from [Dubrovnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubrovnik "Dubrovnik") around 1359, in the 14th-century Vitosha Charter of Bulgarian tsar [Ivan Shishman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Shishman_of_Bulgaria "Ivan Shishman of Bulgaria") and in a [Ragusan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ragusa "Republic of Ragusa") merchant's notes of 1376.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-38) In these documents, the city is called _Sofia_,[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] but, at the same time, the region and the city's inhabitants are still called _Sredecheski_ ([Church Slavonic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Slavonic_language "Church Slavonic language"): срѣдечьскои, "of Sredets"), which continued until the 20th century. The [Ottomans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") came to favour the name **Sofya** ([صوفيه](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%D8%B5%D9%88%D9%81%D9%8A%D9%87 "wikt:صوفيه")). In 1879, there was a dispute about what the name of the new Bulgarian capital should be, when the citizens created a committee of famous people, insisting for the Slavic name. Gradually, a compromise arose, officialisation of _Sofia_ for the nationwide institutions, while legitimating the title _Sredets_ for the administrative and church institutions, before the latter was abandoned through the years.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-39)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f1/Sofia_seen_from_Vitosha_2.jpg/250px-Sofia_seen_from_Vitosha_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sofia_seen_from_Vitosha_2.jpg)

A view of Sofia and its valley from [Vitosha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitosha "Vitosha")

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Sofia-vitosha-kempinski.jpg/250px-Sofia-vitosha-kempinski.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sofia-vitosha-kempinski.jpg)

Winter panorama of Sofia with Vitosha in the background

[Sofia City Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_City_Province "Sofia City Province") has an area of 1,344 km 2,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-40) while the surrounding and much bigger [Sofia Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Province "Sofia Province") is 7,059 km 2. Sofia's development as a significant settlement owes much to its central position in the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"). It is situated in western Bulgaria, at the northern foot of the [Vitosha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitosha "Vitosha") mountain, in the [Sofia Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia_Valley "Sofia Valley") that is surrounded by the [Balkan Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkan_Mountains "Balkan Mountains") to the north. The valley has an average altitude of 550 metres (1,800 ft). Sofia is the second highest capital of the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (after [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid")) and the third highest capital of Europe (after [Andorra la Vella](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andorra_la_Vella "Andorra la Vella") and Madrid). Unlike most European capitals, Sofia does not straddle any large river, but is surrounded by comparatively high mountains on all sides. Three [mountain passes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mountain_pass "Mountain pass") lead to the city, which have been key roads since antiquity, Vitosha being the watershed between [Black](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Sea "Black Sea") and [Aegean Seas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aegean_Sea "Aegean Sea").

A number of shallow rivers cross the city, including the [Boyanska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyanska_reka "Boyanska reka"), [Vladayska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladaya_River "Vladaya River") and [Perlovska](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perlovska "Perlovska"). The [Iskar River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iskar_(river) "Iskar (river)") in its upper course flows near eastern Sofia. It takes its source in [Rila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rila "Rila"), Bulgaria's highest mountain,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Geographic_Dictionary_of_Bulgaria_537-41) and enters Sofia Valley near the village of [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German,_Bulgaria "German, Bulgaria"). The Iskar flows north toward the Balkan Mountains, passing between the eastern city suburbs, next to the main building and below the runways of [Vasil Levski Sofia Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasil_Levski_Sofia_Airport "Vasil Levski Sofia Airport"), and flows out of the Sofia Valley at the town of [Novi Iskar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Novi_Iskar "Novi Iskar"), where the scenic [Iskar Gorge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iskar_Gorge "Iskar Gorge") begins.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Iskar_1-42)

The city is known for its 49 [mineral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spring_(hydrosphere) "Spring (hydrosphere)") and [thermal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_spring "Hot spring") springs. Artificial and dam lakes were built in the twentieth century.

While the 1818 and 1858 earthquakes were intense and destructive, the [2012 Pernik earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Pernik_earthquake "2012 Pernik earthquake") occurred west of Sofia with a [moment magnitude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moment_magnitude_scale "Moment magnitude scale") of 5.6 and a much lower Mercalli intensity of VI (_Strong_). The [2014 Aegean Sea earthquake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Aegean_Sea_earthquake "2014 Aegean Sea earthquake") was also noticed in the city.

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Climate")]

Sofia has a [humid continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_continental_climate "Humid continental climate") ([Köppen climate classification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification")_Dfb_; _Cfb_ if with −3°C [isotherm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isotherm_(contour_line) "Isotherm (contour line)")) with an average annual temperature of 10.9°C (51.6°F).

Winters are relatively cold and snowy. In the coldest days temperatures can drop below −15°C (5°F), most notably in January. The lowest recorded temperature is −31.2°C (−24°F) (16 January 1893).[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-43)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-44) On average, Sofia receives a total snowfall of 98 cm (38.6 in) and 56 days with snow cover.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-45) The snowiest recorded winter was 1939/1940 with a total snowfall of 169 cm (66.5 in).[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-46) The record snow depth is 57 cm (22.4 in) (25 December 2001).[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-47) The coldest recorded year was 1893 with an average January temperature of −10.4°C (13°F) and an annual temperature of 8.2°C (46.8°F).[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-48)

Summers are quite warm and sunny. In summer, the city generally remains slightly cooler than other parts of Bulgaria, due to its higher altitude. However, the city is also subject to heat waves with high temperatures reaching or exceeding 35°C (95°F) on the hottest days, particularly in July and August. The highest recorded temperature is 40.2°C (104°F) (5 July 2000).[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-49) The hottest recorded month was July 2012 with an average temperature of 24.8°C (77°F).[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-50) The warmest year on record was 2024 with an annual temperature of 12.5°C (55°F).[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-51)

Springs and autumns in Sofia are usually short with variable and dynamic weather.

The city receives an average precipitation of 625.7 mm (24.63 in) a year, reaching its peak in late spring and early summer when [thunderstorms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thunderstorms "Thunderstorms") are common. The driest recorded year was 2000 with a total precipitation of 304.6 mm (11.99 in), while the wettest year on record was 2014 with a total precipitation of 1,066.6 mm (41.99 in).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-53)

### Environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Environment")]

The geographic position of the Sofia Valley limits the flow of air masses, increasing the chances of air pollution by particulate matter and [nitrogen oxide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nitrogen_oxide "Nitrogen oxide").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-65) Solid fuel used for heating and motor vehicle traffic are significant sources of pollutants. Smog thus persists over the city as [temperature inversions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inversion_(meteorology) "Inversion (meteorology)") and the mountains surrounding the city prevent the circulation of air masses.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-SG1-66)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-AFP-67) As a result, air pollution levels in Sofia are some of the highest in Europe.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-NYT1-68)

[Particulate matter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Particulate_matter "Particulate matter") concentrations are consistently above the norm.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-AFP-67) During the October 2017 – March 2018 heating season, particulate levels exceeded the norm on 70 occasions;[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-SG1-66) on 7 January 2018, PM10 levels reached 632 μg/m 3,[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-SG2-69) some twelve times the EU norm of 50 μg/m 3.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-70) Even areas with few sources of air pollution, like [Gorna Banya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gorna_Banya "Gorna Banya"), had PM2.5 and PM10 levels above safe thresholds.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-SG2-69) In response to hazardous spikes in air pollution, the Municipal Council implemented a variety of measures in January 2018, like more frequent washing of streets.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-71) However, a report by the [European Court of Auditors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Auditors "European Court of Auditors") issued in September 2018 revealed that Sofia has not drafted any projects to reduce air pollution from heating. The report also noted that no industrial pollution monitoring stations operate in Sofia, even though industrial facilities are active in the city. A monitoring station on Eagles' Bridge, where some of the highest particulate matter values were measured, was moved away from the location and has measured sharply lower values since then.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-72) Particulates are now largely measured by a network of 300 sensors maintained by volunteers since 2017.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-SG1-66) The [European Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Commission "European Commission") has taken Bulgaria to court over its failure to curb air pollution.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-AFP-67)

### Prehistory and antiquity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Prehistory and antiquity")]

The area has a history of nearly 7,000 years,[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-plants-73) with the great attraction of the hot water springs that still flow abundantly in the centre of the city. The [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") village in [Slatina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slatina,_Sofia "Slatina, Sofia") dating to the 5th–6th millennium BC is documented.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-74) Another neolithic settlement was founded in the 3rd–4th millennium BC near the site of the modern [National Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Art_Gallery_(Bulgaria) "National Art Gallery (Bulgaria)"), which has been the traditional centre of the city ever since.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-sofiaculture.bg-75)

The earliest tribes who settled were the [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians")[Tilataei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilataei "Tilataei"). In the 500s BC, the area became part of a Thracian state union, the [Odrysian kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysian_kingdom "Odrysian kingdom") from another Thracian tribe the [Odrysses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odrysses "Odrysses").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-76)

In 339 BC [Philip II of Macedon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Macedon "Philip II of Macedon") destroyed and ravaged the town for the first time.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Routledge-77)

The [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts") tribe [Serdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdi "Serdi") gave their name to the city.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-78) The earliest mention of the city comes from an [Athenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens") inscription from the 1st century BC, attesting _Astiu ton Serdon_, i.e. city of the Serdi.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-79) According to the inscription and to the writings of [Dio Cassius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dio_Cassius "Dio Cassius"), the Roman general [Crassus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crassus "Crassus") subdued the Serdi and behanded the captives.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-80)

Dio Cassius, [Pliny the Elder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Elder "Pliny the Elder") and [Ptolemy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy "Ptolemy") say that in 27–29 BC Crassus attacked the region "Segetike", which is assumed to be [Serdica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serdica "Serdica"), or the city of the Serdi.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-81)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-82)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-83) The ancient city is located between [TZUM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TZUM_(Sofia) "TZUM (Sofia)"), [Sheraton Hotel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheraton_Hotel "Sheraton Hotel") and the Presidency.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-sofiaculture.bg-75)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-84) It gradually became the most important Roman city of the region.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-world-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-books.google.bg-34) It became a _municipium_ during the reign of Emperor [Trajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan "Trajan") (98–117). Serdica expanded, as [turrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turret_(architecture) "Turret (architecture)"), protective walls, [public baths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_bathing "Public bathing"), administrative and cult buildings, a civic [basilica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basilica "Basilica"), an [amphitheatre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre "Amphitheatre"), a circus, the [City council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_council "City council") (Boulé), a large forum, a big circus (theatre), etc. were built. Serdica was a significant city on the Roman road [Via Militaris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Via_Militaris "Via Militaris"), connecting [Singidunum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Singidunum "Singidunum") and [Byzantium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantium "Byzantium"). In the 3rd century, it became the capital of [Dacia Aureliana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacia_Aureliana "Dacia Aureliana"),[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-85) and when Emperor [Diocletian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocletian "Diocletian") divided the province of Dacia Aureliana into Dacia Ripensis (at the banks of the [Danube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danube "Danube")) and [Dacia Mediterranea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacia_(Roman_province) "Dacia (Roman province)"), Serdica became the capital of the latter. Serdica's citizens of [Thracian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thracians "Thracians") descent were referred to as [Illyrians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Illyrians "Illyrians")[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Routledge-77) probably because it was at some time the capital of [Eastern Illyria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Illyria?action=edit&redlink=1 "Eastern Illyria (page does not exist)") ([Second Illyria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Illyria?action=edit&redlink=1 "Second Illyria (page does not exist)")).[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-86)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/20140618_Sofia_09.jpg/250px-20140618_Sofia_09.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20140618_Sofia_09.jpg)

Dated from the early 4th century, the [Church of Saint George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_Saint_George,_Sofia "Church of Saint George, Sofia") is the oldest standing edifice in Sofia.

Roman emperors [Aurelian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aurelian "Aurelian") (215–275)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-87) and [Galerius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galerius "Galerius") (260–311)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-88) were born in Serdica.

The city expanded and became a significant political and economical centre, more so as it became one of the first Roman cities where Christianity was recognised as an [official religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_religion "State religion") (under [Galerius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galerius "Galerius")). The [Edict of Toleration by Galerius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Toleration_by_Galerius "Edict of Toleration by Galerius") was issued in 311 in Serdica by the Roman emperor Galerius, officially ending the Diocletianic persecution of Christianity. The Edict implicitly granted Christianity the status of "[religio licita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religio_licita "Religio licita")", a worship recognised and accepted by the Roman Empire. It was the first edict legalising Christianity, preceding the [Edict of Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Milan "Edict of Milan") by two years.

Serdica was the capital of the [Diocese of Dacia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Dacia "Diocese of Dacia") (337–602).

For [Constantine the Great](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantine_the_Great "Constantine the Great") it was 'Sardica mea Roma est' (Serdica is my Rome). He considered making Serdica the capital of the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") instead of Constantinople.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-89) which was already not dissimilar to a [tetrarchic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrarchy "Tetrarchy") capital of the Roman Empire.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-90) In 343 AD, the [Council of Sardica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Sardica "Council of Sardica") was held in the city, in a church located where the current 6th century [Church of Saint Sophia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia_Church_(Sofia) "Hagia Sophia Church (Sofia)") was later built.

The city was destroyed in the [447 invasion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodosius_II#Wars_with_the_Huns,_Vandals,_and_Persians "Theodosius II") of the [Huns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huns "Huns") and laid in ruins for a century.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Routledge-77) It was rebuilt by [Byzantine Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Byzantine_emperors "List of Byzantine emperors")[Justinian I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I "Justinian I"). During the reign of Justinian it flourished, being surrounded with great fortress walls whose remnants can still be seen today.

### Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Middle Ages")]

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ed/Kalojan_desislava.jpg/250px-Kalojan_desislava.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Kalojan_desislava.jpg)

The 13th century lord of Sredets [Kaloyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaloyan_and_Desislava "Kaloyan and Desislava") and his wife Desislava, [Boyana Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boyana_Church "Boyana Church")

Serdica became part of the [First Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Bulgarian_Empire "First Bulgarian Empire") during the reign of Khan [Krum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Krum "Krum") in 809, after a long [siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Serdica_(809) "Siege of Serdica (809)"). The fall of the strategic city prompted a major and ultimately disastrous invasion of Bulgaria by the [Byzantine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") emperor [Nikephoros I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikephoros_I "Nikephoros I"), which led to his demise at the hands of the [Bulgarian army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medieval_Bulgarian_army "Medieval Bulgarian army").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-91) In the aftermath of the war, the city was permanently integrated in Bulgaria and became known by the Slavic name of Sredets. It grew into an important fortress and administrative centre under Krum's successor Khan [Omurtag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omurtag_of_Bulgaria "Omurtag of Bulgaria"), who made it a centre of Sredets province (Sredetski komitat, Средецки комитат). The Bulgarian patron saint [John of Rila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_of_Rila "John of Rila") was buried in Sredets by orders of Emperor [Peter I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_I_of_Bulgaria "Peter I of Bulgaria") in the mid 10th century.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-stancheva120-92) After the conquest of the Bulgarian capital [Preslav](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preslav "Preslav") by [Sviatoslav I of Kyiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sviatoslav_I "Sviatoslav I") and [John I Tzimiskes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_I_Tzimiskes "John I Tzimiskes")' armies in 970–971, the [Bulgarian Patriarch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriarch_of_All_Bulgaria "Patriarch of All Bulgaria") Damyan chose Sredets for his seat in the next year and the capital of Bulgaria was temporarily moved there.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-93) In the second half of 10th century the city was ruled by [Komit Nikola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_(komes) "Nicholas (komes)") and his sons, known as the "[Komitopuli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cometopuli_dynasty "Cometopuli dynasty")". One of them was [Samuil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_of_Bulgaria "Samuel of Bulgaria"), who was eventually crowned Emperor of Bulgaria in 997. In 986, the Byzantine Emperor [Basil II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basil_II "Basil II") laid siege to Sredets but after 20 days of fruitless assaults the garrison broke out and forced the Byzantines to abandon the campaign. On his way to Constantinople, Basil II was ambushed and soundly defeated by the Bulgarians in the [battle of the Gates of Trajan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Gates_of_Trajan "Battle of the Gates of Trajan").[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-stancheva120-92)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-94)

The city eventually fell to the [Byzantine Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_Empire "Byzantine Empire") in 1018, following the [Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byzantine_conquest_of_Bulgaria "Byzantine conquest of Bulgaria"). Sredets joined the [uprising of Peter Delyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uprising_of_Peter_Delyan "Uprising of Peter Delyan") in 1040–1041 in a failed attempt to restore Bulgarian independence and was the last stronghold of the rebels, led by the local commander Botko.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-95) During the 11th century many [Pechenegs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pechenegs "Pechenegs") were settled down in Sofia region as Byzantine federats.

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3f/StSophiaChurch-Sofia-10.jpg/250px-StSophiaChurch-Sofia-10.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:StSophiaChurch-Sofia-10.jpg)

Interior of the ancient [Saint Sofia Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sofia_Church,_Sofia "Saint Sofia Church, Sofia")

It was once again incorporated into the [restored Bulgarian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Bulgarian_Empire "Second Bulgarian Empire") in 1194 at the time of Emperor [Ivan Asen I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Asen_I_of_Bulgaria "Ivan Asen I of Bulgaria") and became a major administrative and cultural centre.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-96) Several of the city's governors were members of the Bulgarian imperial family and held the title of _[sebastokrator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastokrator "Sebastokrator")_, the second highest at the time, after the [tsar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsar "Tsar"). Some known holders of the title were [Kaloyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaloyan_(sebastocrator) "Kaloyan (sebastocrator)"), [Peter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_(sevastokrator) "Peter (sevastokrator)") and their relative Aleksandar Asen (d. after 1232), a son of [Ivan Asen I of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivan_Asen_I_of_Bulgaria "Ivan Asen I of Bulgaria") (r.1189–1196). In the 13th and 14th centuries Sredets was an important spiritual and literary hub with a cluster of 14 monasteries in its vicinity, that were eventually destroyed by the Ottomans. The city produced multicoloured sgraffito ceramics, jewellery and ironware.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-97)

In 1382/1383 or 1385, Sredets was seized by the [Ottoman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire "Ottoman Empire") in the course of the [Bulgarian-Ottoman Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian%E2%80%93Ottoman_Wars "Bulgarian–Ottoman Wars") by [Lala Şahin Pasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lala_%C5%9Eahin_Pasha "Lala Şahin Pasha"), following a [three-month siege](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Sofia "Siege of Sofia").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-:0-98) The Ottoman commander left the following description of the city garrison: "Inside the fortress [Sofia] there is a large and elite army, its soldiers are heavily built, moustached and look war-hardened, but are used to consume wine and [rakia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rakia "Rakia")—in a word, jolly fellows."[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-99)

### Early modern history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Early modern history")]

From the 14th century till the 19th century Sofia was an important administrative centre in the Ottoman Empire. It became the capital of the [beylerbeylik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beylerbey "Beylerbey") of [Rumelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumelia "Rumelia") ([Rumelia Eyalet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumelia_Eyalet "Rumelia Eyalet")), the [province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Administrative_divisions_of_the_Ottoman_Empire "Administrative divisions of the Ottoman Empire") that administered the Ottoman lands in [Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europe "Europe") (the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans")), one of the two together with the beylerbeylik of [Anatolia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anatolia "Anatolia"). It was the capital of the important [Sanjak of Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjak_of_Sofia "Sanjak of Sofia") as well, including the whole of [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace "Thrace") with [Plovdiv](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plovdiv "Plovdiv") and [Edirne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edirne "Edirne"), and part of [Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(region) "Macedonia (region)") with [Thessaloniki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thessaloniki "Thessaloniki") and [Skopje](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skopje "Skopje").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-100)

During the initial stages of the [Crusade of Varna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusade_of_Varna "Crusade of Varna") in 1443, it was occupied by Hungarian forces for a short time in 1443, and the Bulgarian population celebrated a Mass in [Saint Sofia Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Sofia_Church,_Sofia "Saint Sofia Church, Sofia"). Following the defeat of the crusader forces in 1444, the city's Christians faced persecution. In 1530 Sofia became the capital of the [Ottoman province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Subdivisions_of_the_Ottoman_Empire "Subdivisions of the Ottoman Empire") (beylerbeylik) of [Rumelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumelia "Rumelia") for about three centuries. During that time Sofia was the largest import-export-base in modern-day Bulgaria for the caravan trade with the [Republic of Ragusa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ragusa "Republic of Ragusa"). In the 15th and 16th century, Sofia was expanded by Ottoman building activity. Public investments in infrastructure, education and local economy brought greater diversity to the city. Amongst others, the population consisted of [Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim "Muslim"), [Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_language "Bulgarian language") and [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language") speaking [Orthodox Christians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Orthodox_Church "Eastern Orthodox Church"), [Armenians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armenians "Armenians"), [Georgians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgians "Georgians"), [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") Ragusans, Jews ([Romaniote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romaniote_Jews "Romaniote Jews"), [Ashkenazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ashkenazi_Jews "Ashkenazi Jews") and [Sephardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sephardi "Sephardi")), and [Romani people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romani_people "Romani people").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-:0-98) The 16th century was marked by a wave of persecutions against the Bulgarian Christians, a total of nine became [New Martyrs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Martyrs "New Martyrs") in Sofia and were sainted by the Orthodox Church, including [George the New](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_of_Kratovo "George of Kratovo") (1515), Sophronius of Sofia (1515), George the Newest (1530), [Nicholas of Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St._Nicholas_of_Sofia "St. Nicholas of Sofia") (1555) and Terapontius of Sofia (1555).[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-101)

[![Image 27: Sofia with the clock tower](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Sofia-oberbauer.png/250px-Sofia-oberbauer.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Sofia-oberbauer.png)

Sofia in mid-19th-century

When it comes to the cityscape, 16th century sources mention eight [Friday mosques](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congregational_mosque "Congregational mosque"), three public libraries, numerous schools, 12 churches, three synagogues, and the largest [bedesten](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedesten "Bedesten") (market) of the Balkans.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-:0-98) Additionally, there were fountains and _[hammams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkish\_bath "Turkish bath")_ (bathhouses). [Lady Mary Wortley Montagu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Mary_Wortley_Montagu "Lady Mary Wortley Montagu") noted that the baths were a public gathering place for Sofia's prominent women and served as a kind of [salon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salon_(gathering) "Salon (gathering)"). Most prominent churches such as Saint Sofia and Saint George were converted into mosques, and a number of new ones were constructed, including [Banya Bashi Mosque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banya_Bashi_Mosque "Banya Bashi Mosque") built by the Ottoman architect [Mimar Sinan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mimar_Sinan "Mimar Sinan"). In total there were 11 big and over 100 small mosques by the 17th century.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-103) In 1610 the [Vatican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") established the [See of Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Sofia_and_Plovdiv "Roman Catholic Diocese of Sofia and Plovdiv") for Catholics of [Rumelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rumelia "Rumelia"), which existed until 1715 when most Catholics had emigrated.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-104) There was an important uprising against Ottoman rule in Sofia, [Samokov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samokov "Samokov") and Western Bulgaria in 1737.

Sofia entered a period of economic and political decline in the 17th century, accelerated during the period of anarchy in the Ottoman Balkans of the late 18th and early 19th century, when local Ottoman warlords ravaged the countryside. 1831 Ottoman population statistics show that 42% of the Christians were non-taxpayers in the [kaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaza "Kaza") of Sofia and the amount of middle-class and poor Christians were equal.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-105) Since the 18th century the _[beylerbeys](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beylerbey "Beylerbey")_ of Rumelia often stayed in [Bitola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bitola "Bitola"), which became the official capital of the province in 1826. Sofia remained the seat of a [sanjak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanjak "Sanjak") (district). By the 19th century the Bulgarian population had two schools and seven churches, contributing to the [Bulgarian National Revival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_National_Revival "Bulgarian National Revival"). In 1858 [Nedelya Petkova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nedelya_Petkova "Nedelya Petkova") created the first Bulgarian school for women in the city. In 1867 was inaugurated the first _[chitalishte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chitalishte "Chitalishte")_ in Sofia – a Bulgarian cultural institution. In 1870 the Bulgarian revolutionary [Vasil Levski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasil_Levski "Vasil Levski") established a [revolutionary committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internal_Revolutionary_Organization "Internal Revolutionary Organization") in the city and in the neighbouring villages. Following his capture in 1873, Vasil Levski was transferred and hanged in Sofia by the Ottomans.

### Modern and contemporary history

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Modern and contemporary history")]

During the [Russo-Turkish War of 1877–78](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Turkish_War_(1877%E2%80%931878) "Russo-Turkish War (1877–1878)"), [Suleiman Pasha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suleiman_Pasha_(Ottoman_general) "Suleiman Pasha (Ottoman general)") threatened to burn the city in defence, but the foreign diplomats Leandre Legay, [Vito Positano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vito_Positano "Vito Positano"), Rabbi Gabriel Almosnino and Josef Valdhart refused to leave the city thus saving it. Many Bulgarian residents of Sofia armed themselves and sided with the Russian forces.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-106) Sofia was relieved (see [Battle of Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Sofia "Battle of Sofia")) from [Ottoman rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_rule_of_Bulgaria "Ottoman rule of Bulgaria") by [Russian forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Russian_Army "Imperial Russian Army") under Gen. [Iosif Gurko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iosif_Gurko "Iosif Gurko") on 4 January 1878. It was proposed as a capital by [Marin Drinov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marin_Drinov "Marin Drinov") and was accepted as such on 3 April 1879. By the time of its liberation, the population of the city was 11,649.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-107)

Most mosques in Sofia were destroyed in that war, seven of them destroyed in one night in December 1878 when a thunderstorm masked the noise of the explosions arranged by Russian military engineers.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-FOOTNOTECrampton2006114-108)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-109) Following the war, the great majority of the Muslim population left Sofia.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-:0-98)

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/376bombgroup-bulgaria-01-jun-1944.gif/250px-376bombgroup-bulgaria-01-jun-1944.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:376bombgroup-bulgaria-01-jun-1944.gif)

The [allied bombing of Sofia in World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Sofia_in_World_War_II "Bombing of Sofia in World War II") in 1944

For a few decades after the liberation, Sofia experienced large population growth, mainly by migration from other regions of the Principality (Kingdom since 1908) of Bulgaria, and from the still Ottoman [Macedonia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macedonia_(region) "Macedonia (region)") and [Thrace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thrace "Thrace").

In 1900, the first electric lightbulb in the city was turned on.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-110)

In the [Second Balkan War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Balkan_War "Second Balkan War"), Bulgaria was fighting alone practically all of its neighbouring countries. When the [Romanian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Army "Romanian Army") entered [Vrazhdebna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vrazhdebna "Vrazhdebna") in 1913, then a village 11 kilometres (7 miles) from Sofia, now a suburb,[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Hall97-111) this prompted the [Tsardom of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Bulgaria "Kingdom of Bulgaria") to capitulate.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] During the war, Sofia was overflown by the [Romanian Air Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanian_Air_Corps "Romanian Air Corps"), which engaged on photoreconnaissance operations and threw propaganda pamphlets to the city. Thus, Sofia became the first capital on the world to be overflown by enemy aircraft.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Hall118-112)

During the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_history_of_Bulgaria_during_World_War_II "Military history of Bulgaria during World War II"), Bulgaria declared war on the US and UK on 13 December 1941 and in late 1943 and early 1944 the [US and UK Air forces conducted bombings over Sofia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombing_of_Sofia_in_World_War_II "Bombing of Sofia in World War II"). As a consequence of the bombings thousands of buildings were destroyed or damaged including the Capital Library and thousands of books. In 1944 Sofia and the rest of Bulgaria was occupied by the Soviet [Red Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Army "Red Army") and within days of the Soviet invasion Bulgaria declared war on Nazi Germany.

In 1945, the communist [Fatherland Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatherland_Front_(Bulgaria) "Fatherland Front (Bulgaria)") took power. The transformations of Bulgaria into the [People's Republic of Bulgaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_Bulgaria "People's Republic of Bulgaria") in 1946 and into the Republic of Bulgaria in 1990 marked significant changes in the city's appearance. The population of Sofia expanded rapidly due to migration from rural regions. New residential areas were built in the outskirts of the city, like Druzhba, Mladost and Lyulin.

During the [Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgarian_Communist_Party "Bulgarian Communist Party") rule, a number of the city's most emblematic streets and squares were renamed for ideological reasons, with the original names restored after 1989.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-113)

The [Georgi Dimitrov Mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgi_Dimitrov_Mausoleum "Georgi Dimitrov Mausoleum"), where [Dimitrov's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgi_Dimitrov "Georgi Dimitrov") body had been preserved in a similar way to the [Lenin mausoleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenin_mausoleum "Lenin mausoleum"), was demolished in 1999.

## Cityscape

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Cityscape")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/79/Cathedral_Saint_Alexander_Nevsky_%2823997168458%29.jpg/250px-Cathedral_Saint_Alexander_Nevsky_%2823997168458%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Cathedral_Saint_Alexander_Nevsky_(23997168458).jpg)

A view over central Sofia, with the [Alexander Nevsky Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Nevsky_Cathedral,_Sofia "Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, Sofia") in the foreground and [Vitosha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitosha "Vitosha") in the distance

In Sofia there are 607,473 dwellings and 101,696 buildings. According to modern records, 39,551 dwellings were constructed until 1949, 119,943 between 1950 and 1969, 287,191 between 1970 and 1989, 57,916 in the 90s and 102,623 between 2000 and 2011. Until 1949, 13,114 buildings were constructed and between 10,000 and 20,000 in each following decade.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-book-114) Sofia's architecture combines a wide range of architectural styles, some of which are aesthetically incompatible. These vary from Christian Roman architecture and medieval Bulgarian fortresses to Neoclassicism and prefabricated Socialist-era apartment blocks, as well as newer glass buildings and international architecture. A number of ancient Roman, Byzantine and medieval Bulgarian buildings are preserved in the centre of the city. These include the 4th century [Rotunda of St. George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotunda_of_St._George,_Sofia "Rotunda of St. George, Sofia"), the walls of the Serdica fortress and the partially preserved [Amphitheatre of Serdica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphitheatre_of_Serdica "Amphitheatre of Serdica").

After the Liberation War, knyaz [Alexander Battenberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander,_Prince_of_Bulgaria "Alexander, Prince of Bulgaria") invited architects from [Austria-Hungary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria-Hungary "Austria-Hungary") to shape the new capital's architectural appearance.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Fig._Arts-115)

Among the architects invited to work in Bulgaria were [Friedrich Grünanger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Gr%C3%BCnanger "Friedrich Grünanger"), Adolf Václav Kolář, and [Viktor Rumpelmayer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viktor_Rumpelmayer "Viktor Rumpelmayer"), who designed the most important public buildings needed by the newly re-established Bulgarian government, as well as numerous houses for the country's elite.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-Fig._Arts-115) Later, many foreign-educated Bulgarian architects also contributed. The architecture of Sofia's centre is thus a combination of [Neo-Baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_Revival_architecture "Baroque Revival architecture"), Neo-[Rococo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rococo "Rococo"), [Neo-Renaissance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_Revival_architecture "Renaissance Revival architecture") and [Neoclassicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoclassicism "Neoclassicism"), with the [Vienna Secession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna_Secession "Vienna Secession") also later playing an important part, but it is most typically Central European.

After World War II and the establishment of a [Communist government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_state "Communist state") in Bulgaria in 1944, the architectural style was substantially altered. [Stalinist Gothic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stalinist_architecture "Stalinist architecture") public buildings emerged in the centre, notably the spacious government complex around [The Largo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Largo,_Sofia "Largo, Sofia"), Vasil Levski Stadium, the Cyril and Methodius National Library and others. As the city grew outwards, the then-new neighbourhoods were dominated by many concrete [tower blocks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tower_block "Tower block"), prefabricated panel apartment buildings and examples of [Brutalist architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brutalist_architecture "Brutalist architecture").

After the abolition of [Communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communism "Communism") in 1989, Sofia witnessed the construction of whole business districts and neighbourhoods, as well as modern skyscraper-like glass-fronted office buildings, but also top-class residential neighbourhoods. The 126-metre (413 ft)[Capital Fort](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_Fort "Capital Fort") Business Centre is the first skyscraper in Bulgaria, with its 36 floors. However, the end of the old administration and centrally planned system also paved the way for chaotic and unrestrained construction, which continues today.

### Green areas

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Sofia&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Green areas")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cb/Borisova_gradina_autumn.jpg/250px-Borisova_gradina_autumn.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Borisova_gradina_autumn.jpg)

[Borisova gradina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borisova_gradina "Borisova gradina")

The city has an extensive [green belt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_belt "Green belt"). Some of the neighbourhoods constructed after 2000 are densely built up and lack green spaces. There are four principal parks – [Borisova gradina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borisova_gradina "Borisova gradina") in the city centre and the _Southern_, _Western_ and _Northern_ parks. Several smaller parks, among which the [Vazrazhdane Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vazrazhdane_Park?action=edit&redlink=1 "Vazrazhdane Park (page does not exist)"), [Zaimov Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaimov_Park?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zaimov Park (page does not exist)"), [City Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_Garden_(Sofia) "City Garden (Sofia)") and the [Doctors' Garden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctors'_Garden "Doctors' Garden"), are located in central Sofia. The [Vitosha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitosha "Vitosha") Nature Park (the oldest [national park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_park "National park") in the [Balkans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balkans "Balkans"))[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-116) includes most of [Vitosha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitosha "Vitosha") mountain and covers an area of 266 square kilometres (103 sq mi),[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sofia#cite_note-117) with roughly half of it lying within the municipality of Sofia. Vitosha mountain is a popular hiking destination due to its proximity and ease of access via car and public transport. Two functioning cable cars provide year long access from the outskirts of the city. The mountain offers favourable skiing conditions during the winter. During the 1970s and the 1980s multiple ski slopes of varying difficulty were made available. Skiing equipment can be rented and skiing lessons are available. However, due to the bad communication between the private offshore company that runs the resort and Sofia municipality, most of the ski areas have been left to decay in the last 10 years, so that only one chairlift and one slope work.

Title: First In Situ Identification of Ultradian and Infradian Rhythms, and Nocturnal Locomotion Activities of Four Colonies of Red Wood Ants (Formica rufa-Group)

URL Source: https://harvardforest.fas.harvard.edu/publications/pdfs/Berberich_JBioRhythms_2019.pdf

Published Time: Sun, 25 Jun 2023 19:26:26 GMT

Number of Pages: 20

Markdown Content:
> https://doi.org/10.1177/0748730418821446

JOURNAL OF BIOLOGICAL RHYTHMS, Vol. 34 No. 1, February 2019 19 –38 DOI: 10.1177/0748730418821446 © 2019 The Author(s) Article reuse guidelines: sagepub.com/journals-permissions 19 Geophysical processes, such as the Earth’s 24-h rotation, day-night cycle, tides, and the Moon’s rota-tion, drive all rhythms, and the behavior and survival of life on Earth (Evans and Gorman, 2016; Fuchikawa et al., 2016; Helm et al., 2017). Furthermore, the Earth’s magnetic field has a fundamental period of 24 h that varies somewhat with local time, latitude, sea-son, and solar cycle (Macmillan, 2004). Besides diel fluctuations in environmental conditions and the tilt of the Earth’s axis (approximately 23.4°), geophysical processes are further associated with abiotic cycles, primarily seasonal changes in day length (duration and intensity of the LD cycle) and meteorological cycles (e.g., temperature, air pressure, humidity, precipitation) throughout the year (Daan, 2010; Helm et al., 2017). The temporal organization of molecular, cellular, biochemical, physiological, and behavioral processes are thought to be coordinated by an endogenous, self-sustaining 24-h (circadian) clock, synchronized (entrained) to the daily LD cycle (e.g., Kronfeld-Schor et al., 2013; Sharma, 2003). Under natural conditions, organisms perceive this rhythmic information and generate internal representations of time (Helm et al., 2017). Both LD cycles and temperature are hypothe-sized to be the dominant environmental factors influ-encing the synchronization of circadian clocks and, consequently, the biotic cycle, in organisms from 821446JBRXXX10.1177/0748730418821446JournalofBiologicalRhythms Berberich et al. / In Situ Ultradian And Infradian Rhythms of Red Wood Ants 

> research-article 2019

1.  To whom all correspondence should be addressed: Gabriele M. Berberich, Image Analysis Group, Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, Technical University of Dortmund, Otto-Hahn-Str.4, Dortmund, 44227, Germany; e-mail: gabriele.berberich@tu-dortmund.de. First In Situ Identification of Ultradian and Infradian Rhythms, and Nocturnal Locomotion Activities of Four Colonies of Red Wood Ants ( Formica rufa -Group) Gabriele M. Berberich, 1, * Martin B. Berberich, † Aaron M. Ellison, ‡ Arne Grumpe,* and Christian Wöhler* 

*Image Analysis Group, Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Information Technology, Technical University of Dortmund, Dortmund, Germany, †IT-Consulting Berberich, Erftstadt, Germany, and ‡Harvard Forest, Harvard University, Petersham, MA, USA Abstract  In situ activity patterns of 2 Formica rufa -group species ( F. pratensis; F. polyctena ) were continuously studied at 4 different red wood-ant nests for 6 months in each of the years 2010, 2011, 2012, and 2016 and related to weather factors and variations in the Earth’s magnetic field. The in situ activity patterns of both species were similarly periodic and exhibited ultradian, and short- and long infradian rhythms under natural LD conditions. Crepuscular and nocturnal activities shorter than or equal to 4 h were observed in both species, especially at the new moon and first quarter after the astronomical twilight in a period of darkness in fall. We hypothesize that local variability in the Earth’s magnetic field affects these long-term activity patterns, whereas humidity and temperature were more strongly associated with ultradian rhythms (less than 20 h). 

Keywords  in situ investigation, infradian rhythm, locomotion, magnetic variations, red wood ants ( F. polyctena, F. pratensis ), ultradian rhythm 20  JOURNAL OF BIOLOGICAL RHYTHMS / February 2019 bacteria to animals. These factors can also promote a change in clock phase in either direction depending on time (Cornelissen et al., 1999; Lazzari and Insausti, 2008), which, in turn, can alter the timing of daily behaviors (e.g., rest-activity cycles, mating, egg hatching, feeding). Besides diurnal periodicity (Cornelissen et al., 1999; Gillette and Sejnowski, 2005), there are many other cyclic processes that interact with one another, such as circa-tidal (Satoh and Numata, 2014), reproductive (Houdelier et al., 2002), weekly (Meyer-Rochnow and Brown, 1998; Reinberg at al., 2017), and annual rhythmicity (Bertolucci et al., 2002). Recent studies using model organisms to study circadian behavioral rhythms have highlighted dis-crepancies between rhythms observed under stan-dardized laboratory conditions and those observed in the field (Daan, 2011; Dominoni et al., 2017; Helm et al., 2017; Kronfeld-Schor et al., 2013). Field studies show that various abiotic and biotic parameters influ-ence organisms, including the anticipation of light transitions, twilight activity, nocturnal behavior under moonlight, and the dominance of light over temperature stimuli (e.g., Calisi and Bentley, 2009; Daan, 2011; van der Veen and Gerkema, 2017; Vanin et al., 2012). Consequently, investigations into biolog-ical rhythms in natural environments necessitate common research among multiple disciplines (e.g., biology, geology) in order to understand and explore biological clocks and how they are influenced by abi-otic factors in natural ecosystems. The research described herein focuses on the role of abiotic in situ factors, such as variations in the magnetic field and weather processes, that might influence the organ-ism’s behavior. Social insects, including ants, show social synchro-nization and complex forms of timed behavior and organization within their colonies. Such synchroniza-tion appears to improve coordination among indi-viduals for social integration (Bloch, 2009). “Around the clock” activities have been observed within nests for worker ants involved in brood care (Bloch, Barnes, et al., 2013). In contrast, pronounced diurnal rhythms and well-defined nocturnal periods of sleep were found for foragers outside the nest (Bloch, Hazan, et al., 2013). Further, the mating activities of males and females are coordinated by the timing of nuptial flights to a species-specific time of day, which facili-tates reproductive isolation between species that inhabit the same region (Bloch, 2009; Hölldobler and Wilson, 1990). It has been assumed that task-specific variability in the diurnal rhythms of social insects is adaptive because it improves specialization and col-ony efficiency (Bloch, 2009). Ant queens show a reversible rhythmicity that switches between activi-ties with or without circadian rhythms according to their reproductive status (Bloch, 2009; Eban-Rothschild and Bloch, 2012). Virgin queens adapt to a 24-h rhythmicity, whereas the locomotor activity of mated queens is arrhythmic during the egg-laying period and rhythmically robust afterwards (Sharma et al., 2004); this implies that ant queens have circa-dian clocks that are adaptive and exhibit specific pat-terns of activity that may be influenced by their physiological state or their tasks in the colony. Until now, chronobiology investigations of red wood-ants (RWA), including circadian rhythms of isolated individual workers, foragers, or queens and males of several species of the Formica rufa -group, have been studied mostly in laboratory experiments under standardized artificial LD conditions (Table 1). Laboratory studies with isolated individuals have shown that circadian rhythms are predominantly entrained by light (Fuchikawa et al., 2016) and that periodicity in worker activity depends on tempera-ture or luminosity cycle (Rosengren, 1977; Rosengren and Fortelius, 1986). The mean period of the free-run-ning rhythm of isolated workers (of F. rufa ) was 22.5 (0.45) h for ants placed in constant darkness (DD) and 24.5 (0.33) h for ants placed in constant light (LL), and these ants could be readily entrained by a LD cycle (North, 1987; North, 1993). However, synchroniza-tion of the circadian rhythms was not observed, and this varied considerably among individuals (Nowinszky et al., 1979; Nowinszky, 2004). Chronobiological field studies of RWA are rare, especially ones investigating entire colonies (Rosengren, 1977; Table 1). Our results to date of long-term in situ behavioral field studies— combining geology, geophysics, ecology, and entomology—have shown that 2 RWA species, F. pratensis and F. polyctena ,have well-identifiable daily and bimodal standard daily routines (M-shaped curves) that depend on sea-sons and weather conditions (Berberich et al., 2013). Some major questions still remain unanswered: 1) Is there a co-expression of ultradian, diel, and infra-dian rhythms in an entire colony monitored in situ under natural LD conditions? 2) Are there differences in rhythms between F. pratensis and F. polyctena ? 3) Is there a difference in monthly rhythms? 4) Are astro-nomical and civil twilight functionally significant for activities and do they influence activity patterns? and 5) What new information can be gained by investigat-ing locomotor activities? To understand in situ activi-ties under natural LD conditions, we continually studied long-term the activity patterns of entire colo-nies of these 2 species in situ using 4 nests (Nest 1 [N1]: F. pratensis ; Nests 2 to 4 [N2, N3, N4]: F. polyc-tena ) with a focus on abiotic factors, including varia-tions in the Earth’s magnetic field (e.g., declination, horizontal variation, vertical intensity and total inten-sity) and weather. performed for a period of 6 months (April to September) in 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2016, encompass-ing approximately 15,600 recorded h (approx. 650 d) of video streams. Spring-to-autumn records were automatically evaluated by applying our previously published image evaluation routine, which is based on a difference-image (every 10 sec) technique to obtain an objective interpretation of ant behavior. This is then used to compare directly the activity pat-terns of these 2 species (Berberich et al., 2013).

Red Wood-Ant Nests and In Situ Continuous Monitoring of Activity Patterns 

The 4 RWA nests were located approximately 22 km apart in Weibern (Nest 1; N50.40687 E7.14578; 441 m a.s.l.) and at the Goloring site (Nests 2-4; N50.33976 E7.43955; 318 m a.s.l.). Both study areas were situated west of the Rhine River in the Quaternary East Eifel Volcanic field (EEVF; western Germany). Nest 1 ( F. pratensis ; sunlit, height: 0.90 m; diameter: 1.20 m; monitoring period 04-09/2010 and 2011) was located in a private garden at Weibern. Nest 2 ( F. polyctena ; partly sunlit, height: 0.50 m; diameter: 0.80 m; monitoring period 04-09/2010, Nest 3 ( F. polyctena ; partly sunlit, height: 0.50 m; diameter: 1.00 m; monitoring period 04-09/2012) and Nest 4 ( F. polyctena ; partly sunlit, height: 0.70 m; diameter: 2.20 m; monitored within the research project “GeoBio-Interactions” from 04-09/2016) were located at the Goloring site, an Iron-aged henge sanctuary (GDKE, 2018). In the past, the main selection criteria for the chosen RWA nests had been a seismically active area with degas-sing faults (Berberich et al., 2013; Berberich, et al. 2018a; 2018b). For this reason, these 4 nests were the appropriate choices for studying ant activity pat-terns. During our monitoring periods, long-term in situ data were acquired during field campaigns in which we also studied degassing of geogenic gases (He, Rn, CO2, CH4) and tectonic processes associ-ated with RWA nests in 2010, 2011, 2012 and 2016 (Berberich et al., 2013; 2018a; 2018b). Here, we use these long-term data and associated video footage of RWA colonies to assess ant activity and the pos-sible influences of abiotic geophysical and meteoro-logical processes. Ant activity was continuously monitored using high-resolution camera systems (“AntCams”; Mobotix MX-M12D-Sec-DNight-D135N135; 1,280 × 960 pix-els), installed approximately 5 m from the nests. During the monitoring periods, ant activities on top of the nest were recorded at 12 Hz and continuously time-stamped. Monitoring and automatic evaluation of ant activities was used to ensure an objective inter-pretation of ant behavior, using the approach devel-oped by Berberich et al. (2013). This approach is not based on manually performed counts of single ants on top of the nest but rather applies image difference analysis techniques based on pixel differences. Berberich et al. (2018a) extended the system of Berberich et al. (2013) to compensate for slight camera movements or differences between day and night sen-sors. The network-compatible AntCam was connected to a network-attached storage (NAS) system and a computer to allow for the on-site evaluation of RWA activities in real time using C ++ code to accelerate image evaluation (Berberich et al., 2018a). A total of 15,600 recorded h ( ≈650 d) of video streams were evaluated. 

data Analysis of Video Streams 

We first centered and scaled the data by subtract-ing the mean during the target time and dividing it by the SD. Because the average ant activity produces a large peak in the origin of the amplitude spectrum, this zero frequency component would shadow low frequency components due to the main lobe of the window function and was thus removed. A median filter (width 30) was then applied to the automati-cally evaluated raw data. Then, the data-set was chunked into 5-min data blocks and analyzed for periodicities by applying a modified Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) using Matlab 2017a (www.math-works.com). Because the observation interval corre-sponds to an infinite signal multiplied by a rectangular window, the amplitude spectrum of the signal itself is strongly influenced by the Fourier transform of the window. Consequently, we applied a Blackman win-dow (Oppenheim et al., 1999) to suppress the side lobes of the rectangular window. The approach of Chiu (1989) with an alpha level = 0.05 was used to test for the significance of periodic components in the FFT analysis. 

Locomotion Activity Plots 

For the locomotion activity plots, the 5-min, median-filtered data blocks (288 single data per day; 183 d per monitoring period from 1 April to 30 September; in total, maximum of 212,544 data per investigated year) were normalized to range from 0 (no activity of ants on top of the nest) to 1 (maximum activity of ants on top of the nest) to ensure compa-rable data among all monitored years and nests. Data are graphically displayed using the contour plot function of Matlab2017a. The x-axis of each plot Berberich et al. / IN SITU ULTRADIAN AND INFRADIAN RHYTHMS OF RED WOOD ANTS  23 spans the entire monitoring period and the y-axis shows the time [UTC] from 0000 h to 2400 h. To dis-tinguish between unimodality and bimodality in the locomotion activity plots, we applied Hartigan’s dip statistic (HDS) test (Hartigan and Hartigan, 1985; Mechler, 2002). HDS values ranged from 0 to 1, indi-cating significant bimodality at values <0.05 and bimodality with marginal significance at values between 0.05 and 0.10 (Freeman and Dale, 2012). To detect crepuscular and nocturnal activities between the start and end of civil and astronomical twilight for both ant species, even at low levels, and to obtain comparable results for all 4 nests, y-axis values between 0.5 and 1.0 were taken from the locomotion plots of Figure 3. To investigate the relation of cre-puscular and nocturnal activities to the 4 moon phases (1 st Q =1 st Quarter, FM = Full moon, LQ =

Last Quarter, NM = New Moon), we set a range of 3 d before and after the peak date of each moon phase (in total 7 d). We then summed the activity hours during these 7 d for each moon phase and each nest. A ±1 SD ( ±1σ) boundary was then applied to iden-tify meaningful values. Data for the astronomical and civil twilight for Kobern-Gondorf and Weibern (https://galupki.de/ kalender/sunmoon.php), high-noon (www.time-anddate.de/sonne) and moon-phases (http:// aa.usno.navy.mil) also are noted on the plots; the time of the internal switch between the infrared (night) and color (day) sensors was recorded and is also plotted. Meteorological data (temperature [°C], humidity [%], atmospheric pressure [hpa], and rain-fall [mm]) were recorded by a local in situ meteoro-logical station in 2016, chunked to 10-min data blocks, and analyzed using a modified FFT. Variations in the magnetic field (declination [D], horizontal intensity [H], and vertical intensity [Z] and indepen-dent scalar measurements of total intensity [F]) were recorded by the Adolf-Schmidt-Observatory for Geomagnetism of GFZ German Research Centre For Geosciences, Niemegk (Matzka, 2016; GFZ, 2016; http://www.gfz-potsdam.de/sektion/erdmagnet-feld/daten-produkte-dienste/daten-und-berichte/ minutenmittelwerte-ngk). Data are the best available data according to the INTERMAGNET classifica-tions. For correlation analyses, we extracted the first 100 maximum amplitude values of RWA activities (N1–N4), the magnetic variation components (D, H, Z, F) and the meteorological parameters from the FFT analyses, and assigned the values to every full hour. We then calculated the maximum possible cor-relations. The significance of the correlation coeffi-cient were interpreted according to the method of Hinkle et al. (2009). Maximum activities between the start and end of civil twilight for both ant species were extracted from locomotion plots.

Re SULTS 

Activity Patterns 

The in situ activity patterns in the 4 nests of intact colonies of F. pratensis and F. polyctena were equiva-lently periodic, and exhibited diel, ultradian, and infradian rhythms under natural LD conditions. 

Comprehensive Modified Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) Analyses 

Comprehensive modified FFT analyses for the 6-month observation periods revealed similar and different periodicities for the 2 species, which is also confirmed by the highly positive correlation coeffi-cient ( r = 0.85) for N1 and N2 in 2010. Periods were categorized as ultradian ( <20 h), daily (24 [4] h), semi-daily ( ≈12 h) or infradian ( >28 h) (Mildner and Roces, 2017; Saunders, 2002). Because we monitored ants exposed to the field environment and exogenous processes such as natural light and dark periods and a temperature cycle within 24 h, we cannot discrimi-nate between internally and externally generated daily rhythms. Therefore, we will use the expression “daily” rhythm instead of circadian and “semi-daily” instead of “semi-tidal”. There were no differences between the 2 species in activity rhythms during the entire monitoring period of 183 d (Fig. 1a–e): the main peak was observed at 24 h/25 h (daily); a second lower peak at 12 h (semi-daily; ultradian). Significant ultradian peaks occurred at approximately 18 h and 19 h, respectively ( ≈18/19 h), and at 8, 6, 4, and 3 h, but with lower amplitudes. Noticeable short infradian periodicities were observed at 1.2, 1.6, 1.8, 2.0, 2.2, 2.9 d; and longer ones at 3.2 and 21.3 d. The maxi-mum period observed was 1360 h (57 d) in 2010 (N1) and 816 h (34 d) in 2011 (N1), 2012 (N3), and 2016 (N4). Two peaks corresponding to long peri-ods of 85 d were not significant from a signal pro-cessing perspective and were discarded from further analysis. Analyses of monthly ant activity were similar to the 6-month analyses. Apart from equal ultradian, semi-daily, and daily rhythms (Fig. 2a–e), common infradian rhythms varied by month (Table 2). The 24  JOURNAL OF BIOLOGICAL RHYTHMS / February 2019 maximum period observed was 372 h (15.5 d) in May 2016 (N4) and August 2012 (15 d; N3). Additionally, monthly amplitudes varied in strength and between years (Fig. 2). The summer months (July, August and September) were not always the months with the highest activities. The highest amplitudes for N1 were observed in April, June, and September 2010 (Fig. 2a), and for N3 in April, May, and June 2012 (Fig. 2d). Analysis of Locomotion Activity 

Analysis of locomotion activity showed that the entire colonies of F. pratensis (Fig. 3a, b) and F. Berberich et al. / IN SITU ULTRADIAN AND INFRADIAN RHYTHMS OF RED WOOD ANTS  27 

polyctena (Fig. 3c–e) exhibited mostly bimodal rhythms in ant activity for N1 to N4 during the moni-toring periods (Table 3). Bimodality was lowest in 2012 and 2016 (Table 3); this was also shown in the locomotion plots (Fig. 3d, e). In 2012, the focus of locomotion activity in N2 was shifted to the after-noon for the entire monitoring period (Fig. 3 d); in 2016, the shift in locomotion activity in N4 started in the middle of May (Fig. 3e). Monthly values were also bimodally rhythmic for all nests and monitoring periods (Table 4). In 2010, the highest locomotion activities during the day were recorded in June and August for both species (N1, N2; Fig. 4a, c). In 2011, F. pratensis (N1) showed the highest activity in July (Fig. 4b). In 2012, F. polyctena (N3) had the highest activity from May to August, with a focus on afternoon hours (Fig. 4d), whereas the maximum ant activity in N4 was from April to May, with a strong decline for the rest of the year 2016 (Fig. 4e). During the twilight periods between the start and end of civil and astronomical twilight, crepuscular ant activity was observed in both species and varied between species and among years (Figs. 4 and 5). Maximum locomotion activity, up to 4-h, occurred in May and June in N1, N2, and N4 during the start and end of civil twilight (Fig. 4a-e). In 2010, the highest activities were recorded in August for both species (N1, N2; Fig. 4a, c). In 2011, F. pratensis (N1) showed the highest activity from May to July (Fig. 4b). In 2012 and 2016, F. polyctena (N3, N4) had the highest activity in May (Fig. 4d, e). Nocturnal ant activities up to 4-h were also observed in both spe-cies before the start and after the end of astronomi-cal twilight during the darkest hours in spring and autumn (Fig. 5a-e). During civil twilight, May, August, and September were the most active months for all phases of the moon (Fig. 6a-d). From June to the middle of July (midnight twilight), high ant activities were observed at the new moon and first quarter (N1, N2; Fig. 6d). In 2010, during civil twi-light, F. polyctena activities were 3.5-times as long during the new moon and its 1 st Q (164 h) compared with F. pratensis (48 h) during civil twilight (Fig. 6a, d). The sum of nocturnal activities during the full moon and its last quarter were 3-times longer for F. polyctena (116 h vs. F. prat , 39 h) (Fig. 6b, c). In 2010, during astronomical twilight, August and September were the most active months for all phases of the moon (Fig. 6e-h).
